articles.title: Psychometric Validation of a Deep Learning-based Foreground Speech Detection Algorithm for Everyday Conversation Detection
articles.authors: Amanda Marie Bernal; Johannes Leonhard Klinz; Valeria Pfeifer; David Sbarra; Charles L Raison; Nicole Nugent; Rajat Hebbar; Shrikanth Narayanan; Matthias R. Mehl
articles.abstract: Passive ambient audio sampling bears great potential for objectively measuring daily social activity and its association with wellbeing and health. However, detecting true conversations via human annotation is labor-intensive, and automatic labeling via audio signal processing has thus far only received proof-of-concept validation. Here, we conduct a comprehensive psychometric validation of a deep learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm for conversation activity detection (CAD) from ambient audio sampled with the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) method (Hebbar et al., 2021). We assess the CAD algorithm’s validity as an objective measure of conversation activity using four archival EAR datasets with human ground-truth conversation annotations (N = 566 participants, n = 167,539 audio recordings). Specifically, we evaluate, across the four samples, the degree to which the CAD algorithm converges with human-annotated conversation activity, yields temporal stability estimates of conversation activity, and replicates patterns of external correlates (with demographic, wellbeing, and personality measures) comparable to those derived from human ground-truth annotations. We further compare the distributional properties of conversation activity derived from the CAD algorithm and human ground-truth annotations and use this information for thresholding the algorithm’s continuous conversation activity estimates. Overall, the CAD algorithm evidences strong psychometric properties for estimating conversation activity across a range of participants and study characteristics, suggesting that it is suitable for at-scale deployment to objectively measure daily socializing from passively sampled ambient audio.

articles.title: Replicating patterns of Issue Alignment and Issue Asymmetry
articles.authors: Bart de Bruin; Yijing Chen; Philip Warncke; Dino Carpentras
articles.abstract: Classic opinion dynamics models typically focus on a single opinion or treat them as independent dimensions. Several empirical studies indicate however that attitudes are interdependent and embedded within structured belief systems. These systems exhibit a mix of order and variability that standard opinion dynamics models cannot capture. In this work, we have developed an agent-based model that integrates cognitive consistency pressure with attitude structures to recreate these patterns. Specifically, we test two mechanisms through which agents perceive consistency among opinions: one grounded in issue-level associations, and another based on co-occurrence patterns at the position level. Our simulations show that neither mechanism alone is sufficient to reproduce the empirical complexity of empirical belief systems. However, a hybrid approach combining both mechanisms generates attitude structures that closely resemble empirical data. Our findings highlight the role of social perception in shaping belief systems and suggest a novel modelling pathway for studying ideological polarisation across multiple issue domains.

articles.title: Extreme Response Style Generalizes Across Likert-Type and Visual Analogue Scales
articles.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Malin Müller; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles.abstract: Response styles, such as the tendency to prefer extreme or midpoint response options, are a systematic source of variance in self-report data. Individual differences in response styles are largely consistent across traits and over time, but it is unknown whether they generalize across Likert-type scales and visual analogue scales (VAS). In a preregistered within-subjects study, N = 501 participants completed the HEXACO-PI-R, with two content-balanced item subsets presented on a 7-point Likert-type scale and on a VAS. We modeled extreme and midpoint responding as opposite poles of a single dimension, referred to as extreme response style (ERS), using conceptually aligned models: a partial credit model for the Likert-type items and a beta item response model for the VAS items, each extended by a person-specific ERS parameter. Estimating both models jointly in a Bayesian framework, we found that ERS on Likert-type scales and on VAS was substantially correlated (ρERS = .76, 95% CrI [.68, .83]). Individual differences in ERS thus generalized to a considerable extent across response formats. Choosing VAS instead of Likert-type scales therefore does not avoid the influence of response styles, which should be modeled in VAS data as well.

articles.title: Sense of Agency does not influence Memory: Investigation using Intentional Binding Paradigm
articles.authors: Devavrat Pandey; Aditi Jublie
articles.abstract:
Our study examined how modulating agency through free choice and retrospective cues: temporal delay and spatial congruency, could influence memory for words. Intentional binding (IB) was used as the implicit measure of Sense of Agency (SoA). In Experiment 1, participants pressed a key to display words at varying delays (200 ms, 450 ms, and 700 ms), and spatial congruency of word positions, followed by a surprise recognition memory test. Results indicated that SoA was influenced by time delay but not by spatial congruency, while memory remained unaffected. Contrary to the existing literature of IB, the 200 ms delay showed no binding effect, warranting further investigation into factors affecting intentional binding in short time windows, especially with spatial incongruity in visual modality. Experiment 2 was similar to Experiment 1, with one addition: participants responded yes/no to whether the word appeared in their intended location, exploring how engagement with spatial cues of word appearance influences the SoA. Results for the time delay on SoA were similar, and spatial congruency this time showed a significant effect on SoA. However, recognition memory showed no sensitivity to either factor. These findings suggest that while temporal proximity between action and effect enhances the SoA, spatial congruency matters when participants were asked to reflect upon it. In contrast, recognition memory remains unaffected by these factors, indicating either a dissociation between agency computation and memory encoding processes or competition for mental resources required for agency perception and encoding.
Keywords: sense of agency, intentional binding, recognition memory, cue integration

articles.title: Interindividual Heterogeneity in Distributive Justice Manifests in Behavior, Judgments of Others, and Policy Views
articles.authors: Elijah Paul Galvan; Alan Sanfey
articles.abstract: One of the most fundamental questions that we face across all facets of our social lives is that of how resources ought to be distributed. Recent experimental research suggests there is a high degree of interindividual heterogeneity which determines how we make decisions when faced with these dilemmas. However, the extent to which this heterogeneity may manifest in other facets of social interactions is not yet known. Across two behavioral experiments, we explore three questions using a modified Dictator Game, wherein deciders have access to information necessary to assess both Need and Equity. In Experiment 1 (N = 51), we find that judgments of others’ choices were explained by ‘egocentric perspective-taking’: individuated preferences elicited via behavior explain how people judge others’ decisions. In Experiment 2 (N = 251), we find that – despite not being explained by participants’ stated values – task-elicited distributive preferences corresponded to differences in policy views and political orientation, though not meritocratic perceptions. These findings point to the importance of characterizing individual differences for developing an understanding of distributive justice.

articles.title: The middle school divide: Large socioeconomic inequality in cognitive development in a contemporary cohort of US adolescents.
articles.authors: Nicholas Judd
articles.abstract: Across different countries and contexts, parental socioeconomic status (SES) has been consistently associated with childhood cognitive performance. Differences in cognitive ability predict a variety of meaningful, later-life outcomes, making it paramount to understand cognition’s etiology and potential malleability. Despite this, prior longitudinal work examining the influence of SES on later adolescent cognitive trajectories is mixed – with support for 1) widening differences (whereby children with low and high SES diverge), 2) stable/parallel trends, and 3) lessening differences whereby the gap between low and high SES children decreases. Here, we test these competing developmental dynamics in a large cohort of adolescents (N = 9,760, 4 waves) using cutting-edge nonlinear growth curve modeling. Doing so, we find widening cognitive inequality in the United States and identify early adolescence as particularly salient. Given the wide-ranging impact of interindividual differences in cognitive performance, it is paramount to reduce socioeconomic disparities in childhood.

articles.title: Questionnaires on Bilingualism Converge in Latent Space:  A Multiple Factor Analysis of Seven Bilingualism Questionnaires
articles.authors: Tyler Call; Imola MacPhee; Olivia McColl; Olivia Richard; Gigi Luk; Shanna Kousaie; John A E Anderson
articles.abstract: Bilingualism is a multidimensional, dynamic construct that is challenging to measure. Common bilingualism questionnaires differ in the items they contain, complicating comparisons across studies. Prior work has shown limited content overlap between questionnaire items, but the extent of conceptual, or latent overlap between questionnaires remains unclear. We assessed conceptual overlap among seven bilingualism questionnaires by analyzing participant responses rather than questionnaire content. We administered all seven questionnaires to French-English and English-French sequential bilingual undergraduates. Then, we used multiple factor analysis (MFA) to identify latent dimensions capturing shared variance across questionnaires. MFA identified two latent dimensions, corresponding to L2 usage and L2 history/acquisition, which together accounted for 32% of cross-questionnaire variance. MFA also revealed differences in how each questionnaire (and the constituent items) contributed to the global latent dimensions. These findings suggest that the degree of conceptual overlap between questionnaires may be stronger than item analyses imply. While questionnaires should not be seen as directly interchangeable, their convergence suggests that the diverse measures they employ capture shared aspects of bilingual experience.

articles.title: The Endogenous Aspects of Addiction: Diathesis-Stress Interactions between PID-5 Personality Traits and Socio-Ecological Triggers in Substance Use Disorder Patients from North East India
articles.authors: Angshuman Phukan; Monisha Bailung; Dikhyita Gogoi
articles.abstract: Substance use disorder (SUD) is a global public health crisis, with Northeast India exhibiting disproportionately   high   prevalence   rates.   Traditional   socio-ecological   models    often emphasize  familial  and  environmental  factors  in  SUD  etiology.  This  cross-sectional  study investigated  the  interplay  between  self-reported  triggers,  family  history,  and  pathological personality  traits  among  N=62  male  residents  across  three  rehabilitation  facilities  in  Jorhat, Assam.  Utilizing  the  Personality  Inventory  for  DSM-5  Brief  Form  (PID-5-BF),  findings revealed that Disinhibition and Antagonism are the primary neuro-behavioral drivers of early onset,  severe  polysubstance  use,  and  opioid  endorsement.  Contrary  to  socio-ecological assumptions, familial indicators (parental education and substance use) did not independently predict   severity.   However,   a   significant   diathesis-stress   interaction   emerged:   parental substance  use  exacerbated  polysubstance  severity  exclusively  among  highly  disinhibited individuals. Furthermore, comorbid gambling strongly aligned with intrapsychic triggers and a   psychopathy-spectrum   profile   (high   Detachment/Antagonism,   low   Negative   Affect), indicating  under-stimulation  rather  than  distress.  These  results  highlight  the  necessity  of personality-targeted interventions, demonstrating that systemic family vulnerabilities catalyze severe SUD primarily in the presence of underlying personality pathology

articles.title: Exploring Students’ Generative AI Incorporation in Tasks Requiring Internet Searches and Critical Online Reasoning
articles.authors: Carmen Koehler; Gianluca Romano; Sebastian Gombert; Stefan Küchemann; Jochen Kuhn; Dimitri Molerov; Jan Zottmann; Hendrik Drachsler
articles.abstract: Since the release of ChatGPT, numerous articles emerged discussing the pros and cons of the implementing of generative AI tools in educational settings, and researchers predominantly investigated teachers’ and students’ use of those tools in terms of frequency, context of use, and perception. Little is known about students’ processes and approaches when incorporating generative AI tools in their internet searches. Our main aim is to identify different use patterns when employing generative AI-tools for solving information problems that require internet searches. To this end, we investigate students’ actual generative AI use while solving information problems that require internet searches. In our study, first-year university students were presented with generic as well as domain-specific information problems and were allowed to use the internet to write a concluding statement regarding the problem. Out of the total sample, 37 students used a generative AI-tool for task completion. Focusing on these students, we developed a rating scheme and analyzed the prompting pattern, the process of incorporating the generative AI-tool in the task completion, and whether statements from the generative AI-tool were checked against other information sources on the internet. We identified five different types of use patterns when incorporating generative AI-tools in in the process of solving information problems that require internet searches. Results further show that about half of the students heavily rely on the tool and barely verify its statements, while the other half is more cautious and aware of potential unreliable information.

articles.title: Do grit and self-control cause children’s developmental differences in literacy and numeracy throughout primary school?
articles.authors: Alexandra Starr; Maria Psyridou; Bruno Sauce; Elsje van Bergen
articles.abstract:
Background: Children show substantial differences in literacy and numeracy from early primary school, with long-term consequences for later outcomes. These academic skills are predicted not only by cognitive, but also by non-cognitive skills, such as grit and self-control. Yet, prior research is largely correlational and may be confounded by stable individual differences and shared genetic and environmental factors. Here, we examined the developmental interplay between children’s differences in grit and self-control and their literacy and numeracy achievement.
Methods: Using data from the Netherlands Twin Register (up to N=32,165), we analysed teacher-reported grit, self-control, and parent and teacher reports on literacy and numeracy at 7, 10, and 12 years. To strengthen causal inference, we applied two complementary models: (1) random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPMs), testing within-person effects net of stable between-person differences, and (2) monozygotic (MZ) co-twin control CLPMs, testing whether associations persisted after accounting for shared genetic and environmental confounding at the family level. 
Results: We confirmed strong positive between-person associations of grit and self-control with literacy and numeracy (r=.50–.76). Nevertheless, within-person and MZ co-twin cross-lagged effects were substantially attenuated (β = -.21–.14), with few paths reaching significance. We found modest correspondence between the two approaches, indicating that they capture partly distinct sources of confounding rather than one imposing per se stricter control.
Conclusions: Children with higher grit and self-control tend to perform better in school, but our findings provide little evidence that these non-cognitive skills robustly drive later learning. Instead, observed associations appear to largely reflect stable individual differences and familial confounding, underscoring the value of triangulating quasi-experimental designs. 

Keywords: non-cognitive skills; self-regulation; academic achievement; genetically informed design; co-twin control; causal inference

articles.title: Digital news consumption as an information foraging problem
articles.authors: Henrique M. Borges; Ahmed elhady
articles.abstract: News feeds are digitally available all around us, yet the cognitive mechanisms by which we decide what to spend time on, and what to skip, are not well understood. We formulate digital news consumption as an information foraging problem. In this formulation, users move between news articles, formalized as information patches, exploited them like agents consuming food in a canonical patch foraging task. The switching time between news article can be seen as a navigational process that happens at a time akin to the travel time in the canonical patch foraging formalism. To unravel mechanisms determining news reading times, we fit an evidence-accumulation model separately to each of 2,820 readers of a Norwegian newspaper across 1.9 million reads. Reading times are described by accumulation from a variable starting point, in which readers arrive already partly informed. We also show that readers can be divided into two groups reflecting different behavioral patterns that we name: committed and conditional reflecting different distributions of the fitted evidence accumulation model parameters. Our study opens up the opportunity to study the detailed cognitive mechanisms underlying news consumption and our preliminary analysis show that our information foraging approach can be generalized to our types of digital media human interact with on a daily basis.

articles.title: Dynamic Assessment of Narrative in Cantonese: A Study of Classification Accuracy
articles.authors: Li Sheng; Jinghong Ning; Miriam W. L. Chan; Douglas Petersen
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Dynamic assessment shows high discriminant validity in classifying children with and without language disorders across languages and task domains, but studies in non-Indo-European languages are rare. We adapted the language subtest of the Predictive Early Assessment of Reading and Language (PEARL) (Petersen & Spencer, 2014) into the Dynamic Assessment of Narrative in Cantonese (DANIC) and examined the classification accuracy of the prototype DANIC tool in a group of Cantonese-speaking children, as an initial validation before implementing the tool in multilingual Cantonese populations. 
Method: Sixty-one children participated. Thirty-nine met inclusionary criteria and were included in the final analyses, including 16 with language disorders (LD) and 23 typically developing (TD) peers. Children were administered a hearing screen, the DANIC, which consists of a pre-test, a teaching phase, and a post-test, as well as standardised tests of language and nonverbal IQ. 
Results: Pre-test, post-test, and modifiability scores from the DANIC showed significant group differences, but gain scores did not. Logistic regression and Receiver Operating Characteristic analyses identified the overall modifiability rating as the most parsimonious classifier: a rating of 2 or lower on the 0–4 scale identified children with LD with a sensitivity of 93.8% and a specificity of 91.3%. Adding post-test scores raised specificity to 95.7% but did not significantly improve model fit. 
Conclusion: The DANIC is efficient and can be administered with high fidelity and scored reliably. Future studies should examine the utility of this tool in assessing multilingual children from Hong Kong and other Cantonese-speaking regions.

articles.title: Problem gambling and physical blind box and card pack and digital loot box spending: a Mainland Chinese survey
articles.authors: Leon Y. Xiao; Loïs Fournier; Charlotte Eben
articles.abstract: Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling but are generally not regulated as gambling. Virtual gambling-like products include video game loot boxes, whilst physical gambling-like products include blind boxes and card packs. Stakeholders are concerned about the potential harms of these globally popular products, including overspending and the normalization of gambling amongst children. We surveyed Mainland Chinese video game players (final N = 913) to investigate whether spending on various gambling-like products is associated with problem gambling severity. Replicating previous results, we found weak—but practically meaningful—associations between problem gambling severity and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending. In contrast, the association between problem gambling and physical blind box spending was very weak and arguably not practically meaningful. Fundamental differences at the product characteristic-level mean that some gambling-like products, like blind boxes, may be less risky, but further research is warranted. Thus, a cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products. Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a greater potential for harm. Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYFQV (date of in-principle acceptance: 18 March 2026).

articles.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a large number of surveys being distributed was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles.title: Machine Learning and NLP for Multilevel Mental Health Factors in Population Crises: Scoping Review
articles.authors: Ridwan Monjur; Siti Hafiza Hafiza Abd Hamid; NUR NASUHA BINTI MOHD DAUD; Sheri Jahan Chowdhury
articles.abstract:
Background: Pandemics, armed conflicts, natural-hazard disasters, and economic
upheavals are increasingly common and cause long-term psychological harm. We mapped
the mental health determinants that machine learning and natural language processing
studies identify in these crises.

Methods: Following a protocol registered on the Open Science Framework, we searched
PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore on 4 July 2026. We inde-
pendently screened 4,962 records and 132 full-text reports and included 63 studies (11
text-based, 52 survey-based). We coded each study’s top six features with a taxonomy
combining the World Health Organization social determinants framework with social and
psychosocial models.

Results: The taxonomy coded 312 of 317 factor items (98.4%), and we grouped 225 of
them into 31 factor families. Negative constructs led. Life Events (35 items; adverse occur-
rences such as trauma; crisis and trauma exposure family) ranked first, ahead of Chronic
Strains (30; ongoing hardship; worry about infection). Cumulative Physiological Burden
(29; poor health, sleep, and somatic symptoms; poor physical health and poor sleep) came
third. Positive constructs were fewer, led by Mastery & Self Concept (28; beliefs about
control and meaning; hope and optimism). Coping (19; adaptive coping versus substance
use), Bonding Social Capital (18; family support versus bereavement), and Bridging Social
Capital (15; social support and networks) were nearly balanced. Their direction depended
on whether the resource was present or missing. Pandemics centered on chronic uncer-
tainty, armed conflicts on trauma and prior psychiatric burden, natural-hazard disasters on
housing loss, and economic upheavals on financial hardship.

Conclusions: Computational crisis research mainly detects proximal, adverse constructs
that surface after distress has occurred. Protective resources, structural context, economic
upheaval, and natural language processing remain understudied, especially for armed con-
flict. Future work could use large language models to find protective constructs in text,
knowledge graphs to link data to the taxonomy, and explainable AI to record each feature’s
direction.

articles.title: Should I stay or should I go? How social contexts and platform governance shape relational autonomy in AI companionship: A conceptual framework
articles.authors: Ceren Su Abacioglu
articles.abstract:
AI companions can offer emotional reassurance when human support is difficult to reach, but sustained reliance may narrow
human relationships and expose users to abrupt platform changes. Emotional value alone does not show whether a person
can renegotiate or leave an AI bond. This paper examines that question through relational autonomy, defined as a person’s
practical capacity to shape or end an emotionally meaningful AI relationship while retaining viable human alternatives. It
distinguishes usage frequency (engagement) and perceived closeness (relational significance) from structural barriers to leav-
ing (constrained reliance). These distinctions help explain how the same system can produce different outcomes as users’
circumstances and platform designs interact. Relational trajectories may diverge according to users’ social and developmen-
tal circumstances, which shape both the appeal of AI companionship and the availability of meaningful human alternatives.
Providers shape users’ practical agency when they change a companion’s memory, behavior, or availability with limited
user input, making governance rules for ongoing consent, behavioral continuity, and accountability relevant. Hybrid and
decentralized architectures may redistribute data control, though their psychological and equity effects remain unverified.
Evaluating AI companionship therefore requires assessing whether platform rules and offline conditions preserve realistic
relational choices over time.

articles.title: People-Pleasing at Work: Self-Endangering Work Behaviour as a Mechanism Linking People-Pleasing to Emotional Exhaustion
articles.authors: Christian Blötner; Johanna Werner
articles.abstract: People-pleasing reflects a dispositional tendency to prioritize others’ needs and expectations over one’s own, often at personal cost. Such excessive self-neglect arguably increases vulnerability to occupational strain. This study (n = 902 participants working at least 20 hours per week) examined whether people-pleasing is associated with emotional exhaustion and whether this relationship is mediated by behaviours reflecting work-related self-neglect (presenteeism, working during free time, and intensifying and extending work). Structural equation modelling revealed that people-pleasing was positively associated with emotional exhaustion and with all three forms of work-related self-neglect. Presenteeism and intensifying and extending work were positively related to emotional exhaustion and significantly mediated the association between people-pleasing and emotional exhaustion. In contrast, working during free time did not constitute a significant indirect pathway. These findings suggest that people-pleasing may represent a previously overlooked risk factor for occupational strain. Employees high in people-pleasing appear more likely to engage in self-endangering work behaviours that undermine recovery and contribute to emotional exhaustion. Identifying people-pleasing as an antecedent of self-sacrificing work behaviour may inform interventions aimed at promoting employee wellbeing and preventing burnout.

articles.title: Local information and expectations about new ties shape the collective value of social networks
articles.authors: Hicham DAHMOU; Frédéric Moisan; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Social networks emerge from individual decisions to create and remove connections. How can these decentralized decisions produce efficient networks when individuals observe only part of the evolving structure and the first link costs its sponsor more than it returns? Here, we develop an agent-based model of strategic network formation in which agents combine local network information, optimistic expectations about unseen connections, and probabilistic choice. Across groups of 10, 50, and 100 agents, we identify conditions under which near-optimal collective welfare emerges from isolation, despite individual incentives favoring an initially disconnected network. When agents could see only their immediate neighbors, collective welfare peaked at intermediate optimism. A wider view generally broadened the range of optimism compatible with high welfare. Comparisons of individual decisions suggest why: optimism can make the first link attractive, while greater visibility helps agents recognize when a link preserves access and when another route makes it redundant. The starting network also mattered. Some policies that yielded high average welfare from dense random networks yielded lower welfare from both isolation and connected trees. The same fixed decision rule can therefore support both initial linking and subsequent reorganization as the evolving network changes what agents see and which actions they judge worthwhile.

articles.title: Validating log data indicators of acquiring information in critical online reasoning using eye-tracking data
articles.authors: Jannick Illmann; Yavuz Dinc; Carolin Hahnel; Jochen Kuhn; Stefan Küchemann; Verena Ruf; Maruschka Weber; Frank Goldhammer
articles.abstract: Log data can provide opportunities to measure digital skills. However, the interpretation of log data-based indicators comes with a degree of uncertainty. Eye-tracking data can be used to gain convergent validity for log data-based indicators. We illustrate this approach for Online Information Acquisition (OIA), a facet of Critical Online Reasoning, examining four indicators in 26 students completing an online information task. We defined Areas of Interest around snippets on search engine results pages (SERPs) and assessed correlations between indicators and eye-tracking metrics. Results varied by indicator, with time and scrolling on SERPs being positively associated with the median number of snippets fixated, while other indicators were not significantly associated with corresponding metrics. One indicator could not be assessed as it showed no variation in the sample. Findings provide preliminary evidence for a subset of OIA indicator interpretations and underlines the importance of validation when employing log data-based indicators.

articles.title: Determining the perceived utility and veracity of online product reviews: the Consumer Review Evaluation Model (CREM)
articles.authors: Michelle Walther; Sina Frerichs; Steven James Watson; Alexander Boden; Marielle Stel
articles.abstract: When shopping online consumers are frequently confronted with fake reviews. The consequences for the consumers are purchasing flawed, low-quality or even dangerous products. Therefore, to develop effective countermeasures, we need to understand how consumers evaluate the veracity of reviews when making product choices. Thus far, attempts to develop theories about how consumers evaluate review veracity have been based on laboratory or retrospective studies. Therefore, we used thinking-aloud methodology with interactive researcher prompting to more directly observe consumer decision-making regarding the evaluation of consumer reviews. We observed that participants use consumer reviews as a source of information about products. We identified three interrelated judgements in participants’ evaluation of online reviews: review relevance, reviewer credibility, and perceived review veracity. During each judgement participants alternated between heuristic and more systematic processing of deception cues, such as wording, depending on the level of suspicion they trigger. If an evaluation indicated that a review is irrelevant, unbelievable, or untrue, it was not used in the purchase decision process. We integrated our findings from the directly observed decision-making process with existing theory to create an overarching model of human perception of review veracity within the context of an authentic shopping simulation.

articles.title: Ideological Polarization of Moral Sentiment and Framing in US Media: A Multi-Textual Analysis of the Israel–Hezbollah Conflict
articles.authors: Faiqal Dima Hanif; Haidar Buldan Thontowi
articles.abstract: This study aims to detect polarization of moral sentiment based on ideology in United States left- and right-wing media through moral sentiment analysis and topic modeling in the context of the Israel–Hezbollah (Lebanon) conflict. Moral sentiment analysis was conducted using the extended Moral Foundation Dictionary, followed by a two-tailed independent samples t-test to examine moral sentiment differences between the two media groups. Additionally, topic modeling was employed to explore dominant themes across the articles. The findings indicate that both groups of media exhibit negative moral sentiment toward the conflict; however, left-wing outlets demonstrate a higher degree of negative moral sentiment compared to their right-wing counterparts. Additionally, distinct topical patterns emerged, including themes related to refugees, ceasefire, and terrorist threat. These results provide empirical evidence of moral judgement polarization in US media coverage, particularly in moral sentiment expression and topic framing, as shaped by ideological orientation.

articles.title: Audience engagement in live and recorded performance: a social liveness perspective
articles.authors: Robin Ren; Joseph Devlin; John S Hogan; Jorina von Zimmermann; Helen Nuttall; Daniel C. Richardson
articles.abstract: The best memories in life are often collective, from the roar of a stadium to the applause in a concert hall. The value of those moments can be seen in ratings of engagement, feelings of social affiliation, and synchronies in behaviour and autonomic arousal. But what exactly produces the value of the collective experience of a performance? Is it the presence of performers (physical liveness), the presence of other audience members (social liveness), or the fact they are sharing a stimulus? We looked at a range of collective experiences from live theatre to public cinemas to small group viewing in which we varied the two dimensions of liveness and tracked engagement through physiological synchrony. Our goal was to explore some of the many elements that contribute to liveness and engagement. We found that higher liveness, whether physical or social, fostered higher audience engagement and elevated heart rate synchrony. However, co-present pairs were not always more synchronised than pseudo-pairs who watched the same narrative stimuli at different times, suggesting that collective entrainment is not a uniform consequence of ‘being together’. We argue that while many dimensions of sociality might contribute to social liveness, understanding how they combine, how they are balanced with the narrative stimuli to foster collective entrainment without being distracted is the key to creating an engaging collective experience.

articles.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
articles.authors: Andrey Vyshedskiy
articles.abstract: Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

articles.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: Heterogeneity in literacy profiles among adolescents and young adults: a multidimensional person-centered perspective to dyslexia
articles.authors: Elise Lefèvre; Lynne G. Duncan; Ardanouy; Abdessadek El AHMADI; Pascale Colé; Eddy Cavalli
articles.abstract: Purpose: The present study has two aims: to identify literacy profiles based on text reading efficiency, spelling, and reading comprehension in adolescents and young adults with and without dyslexia, and to determine whether cognitive and linguistic predictors differ across profiles. Method: A total of 199 native French speakers aged 15-30 years (104 with dyslexia, 95 typical readers) completed standardized literacy, cognitive, and linguistic tests. We used k-means clustering and multiple regression analyses. Results: Four profiles emerged: proficient and impaired (i.e., high vs. low scores in all domains), resilient (i.e., low text reading efficiency and spelling but preserved comprehension), and poor comprehender (i.e., the reverse pattern). Phonological awareness predicted text reading efficiency and spelling in most profiles, whereas vocabulary predicted reading comprehension only in resilient and proficient profiles. Conclusions: These findings suggest that literacy profiles extend beyond diagnostic categories and rely on distinct mechanisms, which calls for individualized assessments and intervention.

articles.title: Is it Loneliness or Misfit? – Disentangling Predictors of Populist Attitudes and Voting  Intentions
articles.authors: Alma-Sophia Merscher; Anja S. Göritz; Janosch Schobin
articles.abstract:
Loneliness has been associated with various so-called "anti-democratic" attitudes and behaviors 
such as populist voting intentions, voting abstention, and populist attitudes. However, several 
other constructs pertaining to feelings of social disconnection conceptually overlap with 
loneliness and have similarly been linked to anti-democratic outcomes. Among those constructs
are perceptions of being a societal misfit—feelings of not fitting in with the cultural 
mainstream—that have been positively associated with voting abstention. Hitherto it was
unclear whether loneliness uniquely explains populist voting intention, voting abstention, and 
populist attitudes, or whether these associations are better accounted for by perceptions of 
societal misfit. In three online studies (ntotal = 3,017), we tested whether loneliness and misfit 
are empirically distinct and whether they uniquely predict these outcomes. Factor analyses 
suggested that loneliness and misfit are related but distinct constructs. Although both constructs 
significantly the measured predicted political outcomes when considered separately in most 
samples, only misfit retained unique predictive power when both were modeled jointly. These 
findings underscore the importance of disentangling related constructs pertaining to perceived 
social disconnection when explaining political outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Business-size bias in consumer dishonesty: People are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones
articles_hidden.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hallgeir Sjåstad; Helge Thorbjørnsen
articles_hidden.abstract: Consumer dishonest behavior—such as insurance fraud and retail theft—costs businesses billions of dollars every year. Are some businesses more likely to be cheated than others? While classic philosophical perspectives contend that moral transgressions—like dishonesty—are equally wrong regardless of the victim, we suggest that people perceive small organizations as more victim-like than big organizations, which increases the moral cost of cheating small organizations. Supporting this hypothesis, six main and eight supplemental studies (N = 10,436) reveal that people are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, a robust effect across both scenario-based and incentive-compatible experiments. Further, people perceive small businesses as more vulnerable and moral than big businesses, which mediates lower dishonesty toward small businesses. Finally, enhancing big business’ vulnerability and morality can reduce dishonesty toward them. Thus, beyond financial incentives and internal moral standards, dishonest behavior is also shaped by characteristics of the victim.

articles_hidden.title: Flavour through the lens of conflict
articles_hidden.authors: Alice Albertini Drew; Massimiliano Zampini; Salvador Soto-Faraco
articles_hidden.abstract: For many, flavour is the quintessential multisensory experience. It emerges from synthesizing information across sensory modalities and temporal scales. Disparities between these cues are inevitable, and regulation is necessary to synthesize a unitary flavour percept, triggering hedonic and attentional responses, and ultimately liking. Although several frameworks address specific consequences of flavour incongruity, an integrative account unifying perceptual, attentional, hedonic, and adaptive responses remains poorly specified. Here, we explore whether the principles of conflict monitoring, originally developed to explain sensorimotor competition, can be extended to explain the dynamics of competition between flavour-related perceptual representations. We argue that brain mechanisms that monitor for, signal, and regulate discrepancies in information processing can help explain how incongruent flavour cues are resolved, how attention and hedonic responses are modulated, and how flavour representations are updated through experience. This framework is complementary with existing accounts based on predictive processing, causal inference, associative learning, and assimilation–contrast, by specifying when unresolved competition between flavour representations recruits attentional control and adaptive learning. Considering the role of conflict mechanisms in flavour can provide some unification across existing accounts and suggest avenues for research both in the laboratory as well as in the consumer industry.

articles_hidden.title: Fifty Shades of Well-Being: Addressing an Overlooked Source of Confusion in the Science of Well-Being.
articles_hidden.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite constant progress, the science of well-being remains marked by confusion, with a proliferation of competing conceptual frameworks, theoretical approaches, and measurement tools undermining both scientific progress and real-world applications in areas such as counseling, therapy, and public policy. This paper identifies an overlooked contributor to this confusion: the adoption of Philosophically Dense Concepts (PDC) into empirical science, facilitated by academic practices that favor theoretical novelty and discourage interdisciplinary collaboration. Using a conceptual genealogy of the hedonic-eudaimonic well-being distinction as a paradigmatic example, I show how such PDC, when translated from philosophy into psychology and social and health sciences, became semantically fuzzy and led to inconsistent theoretical frameworks and measurement tools. The paper concludes with recommendations on how to better deal with PDC in well-being research and the emerging science of flourishing.

articles_hidden.title: From Preprocessing to Interpretation: Current Practices of Machine Learning in Psychological Research
articles_hidden.authors: Jan Radek; Carolin Strobl; Rosa Lavelle-Hill; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: The application of machine learning methods is becoming increasingly widespread across psychology and related disciplines. However, there is limited knowledge of how and for what purposes researchers employ machine learning to analyze psychological data. To investigate the extent and form in which machine learning is applied in psychological research, we developed a structured description framework that consists of five major steps: (1) data assessment and preprocessing, (2) model fitting, (3) identifying informative variables, (4) interpreting their relationship with the outcome variable, and (5) reporting. Using this framework, we systematically examined current practices employed in psychological and psychiatric research articles published in 2022 and between June 2024 and May 2025 that used one or more of three widely applied supervised machine learning models (specifically, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks) for data analysis. We observed that the majority of researchers (1) used low-dimensional data typical for the psychological field, despite the fact that a particular advantage of machine learning methods is their ability to deal with high-dimensional data, (2) performed a variety of model fit evaluation approaches using cross-validation and train-test splits, which are important strategies for avoiding overfitting, (3) used machine learning approaches to identify informative variables, but (4) did not use the full potential of interpretable machine learning techniques for interpreting the relationship between these variables and the model’s outcome. Furthermore, we observed incoherent reporting practices of machine learning analyses (5). Although first reporting recommendations for machine learning in psychology exist, they have yet to be consolidated into field-wide standards that researchers routinely follow.

articles_hidden.title: Tuned by Experience: Auditory statistical regularities shape attentional prioritization across pitch and timbre
articles_hidden.authors: Jason A Davis; Douglas A Addleman; Kevin Ortego; Viola S. Störmer
articles_hidden.abstract: Listeners navigate complex acoustic environments by selectively attending to relevant sounds amid competing noise. This capacity is classically attributed to top-down goals and bottom-up salience, but recent work implicates a third influence: selection history, whereby incidental exposure to statistical regularities shapes attentional prioritization. We investigated how incidental experience of selecting specific acoustic features influences attentional prioritization across different levels of auditory processing. Participants listened to two concurrently presented sounds to detect a target that contained a brief temporal gap. Unbeknownst to the participants, during a learning phase, one sound was more likely to contain the target gap; in a subsequent testing phase all sounds were equally likely to be the target. Experiment 1 used pure tones of varying pitches, and Experiment 2 used instrument chords (piano, trumpet, guitar). Across both experiments, participants responded faster to high-probability targets during learning, indicating facilitated attentional selection based on the statistical regularities across different levels of acoustic representations. This response time advantage persisted robustly throughout the unbiased testing phase for Experiment 1, but less so for Experiment 2, suggesting that the persistence of experience-driven auditory attention may depend on the complexity of the learned feature. Overall, our findings parallel selection-history effects observed in vision, providing evidence that similar influences of incidental experience on attentional priors exist across sensory modalities.

articles_hidden.title: Meta-learning attentional strategies in multidimensional reinforcement learning
articles_hidden.authors: Mina Habibi; Zhang Chen; Miklos Bognar; Senne Braem
articles_hidden.abstract:
Reward learning in complex, multidimensional environments requires balancing abstract
generalisation with stimulus-specific precision. Previous work suggests that humans initially
rely on feature-based abstraction to support fast generalisation, before shifting toward more
precise, object-based learning. We asked whether humans also generalise these attentional
strategies to novel contexts. In a large-scale study (N = 350), participants learned reward
contingencies in an environment where one feature dimension (colour or pattern) was informative
at a group level but imperfectly predictive at the stimulus level. In a subsequent phase with
novel stimuli, the informative dimension either remained stable (Repeat) or changed (Switch).
Average accuracy performance was similar between conditions, yet computational modelling
revealed a divergence in strategy: when the relevant dimension remained stable, participants
maintained a hybrid approach; when it switched, participants showed a tendency toward object-
based learning, reducing reliance on feature-based abstraction. Time-resolved analyses showed
that this reconfiguration began almost immediately upon entering the new context. Humans
therefore tune the level of abstraction they use based on inferred environmental reliability,
striking a balance between rapid generalisation and stimulus-specific precision

articles_hidden.title: The Feeling of Leaving the Body: A Phenomenological Study of Out-of-Body Experiences in Numadelic VR Near-Death Simulations
articles_hidden.authors: Catherine Andreu; Alejandro Troncoso; Joana Vidal; Oscar Lecuona; Valerie Bonnelle; Joe Hardy; Jose Montemayor; Justin Wall; David Glowacki
articles_hidden.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) can reliably reproduce structural features of the out-of-body experience (OBE), a state linked to lasting shifts in how people relate to their own mortality, yet existing work relies almost entirely on closed-form questionnaires, leaving open how this experience actually feels, and whether it is experienced differently for people confronting a life-threatening illness versus healthy volunteers (HVs). We examined the OBE phase of Clear Light Essence (CLE), a single-session contemplative numadelic VR intervention whose aesthetic is designed to reproduce near-death experience (NDE) phenomenology. Self-report measures in 58 participants (19 patients, 39 HVs) collected before and after the session showed significant, large improvements in mental health, death anxiety, non-dual awareness, and self-related pictographic ratings across both groups. Individual, phenomenologically-informed interviews conducted after the session identified 91 codes organized into four categories (self-environment structure, presence, affective-bodily tone, and ways of attunement), which converged into four distinct experiential structures: rational disconnection, distressed connection, calm connection, and attenuated self. Overall depth of dissolution did not differ between groups, but corporality did: patients more often described a defensive, clinging relationship to the body, even when their broader experience dissolved as deeply as that of controls. This experiential structure correlated strongly with independent markers of self-transcendence, including non-dual awareness and pictographic self-boundary ratings, supporting its validity as a measure of experiential depth. These findings suggest that a brief, numadelic VR-induced OBE engages patients and controls through a largely shared phenomenological architecture, with bodily relation as the primary axis of difference between the two groups.

articles_hidden.title: Criterion-level invisibility in food addiction research: A meta-scientific audit of reporting and interpretation in Yale Food Addiction Scale 2.0 studies
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Goldmann; Isabella Tomlinson; Tamanna Yasmeen; Kareen Kafity; Amelie Christie; Christopher D Chambers
articles_hidden.abstract: Food addiction is increasingly invoked to explain compulsive overconsumption of highly processed foods, and its evidence base rests largely on the Yale Food Addiction Scale 2.0 (YFAS 2.0). It scores 11 criteria adapted from DSM-5 substance use disorder, yet studies commonly report only a food addiction classification, symptom count or severity band. We examined whether the criteria underlying these summaries, including tolerance and withdrawal, are visible in the published record, and whether mixed results are interpreted in a balanced way. Seventy-eight empirical studies administering the full 35-item YFAS 2.0, identified through PubMed, were double-coded according to a preregistered protocol. Sixty-seven studies (85.9%, 95% CI [76.5, 91.9]) did not report all 11 criteria, and 64 (82.1%) reported none; these same 64 omitted both tolerance and withdrawal. Of 69 studies with mixed results, 29 (42.0%, [31.1, 53.8]) drew conclusions that did not reflect that mix, including 6 of the 10 complete reporters with mixed results, and all 29 emphasised significant findings. These results do not show that food addiction is invalid or that unreported symptoms were absent; however,  they indicate that readers can rarely see which symptoms produce a classification, and that interpretation of mixed findings emphasises statistically significant results. Criterion-level reporting and balanced interpretation are separate problems requiring separate remedies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for YFAS 2.0 research.

articles_hidden.title: Is there an autistic voice? A longitudinal study of conversational acoustics, development and individual skills in autistic and non-autistic children
articles_hidden.authors: Riccardo Fusaroli; Christopher Martin Mikkelsen Cox; Ethan Weed; Balázs István Szabó; deborah fein; Letitia Naigles
articles_hidden.abstract:
Atypical prosody is a recognized clinical feature of autism and has been widely investigated as a potential marker for automated screening. However, findings have been difficult to replicate across languages and tasks, raising questions about whether there is a generalizable “autistic voice.” We asked whether acoustic differences vary with children’s development and individual skills, rather than reflecting diagnosis alone. We analyzed 376 US English semi-structured parent–child home interactions collected across six visits over two years from 32 autistic children (mean age at first visit 32.7 months) and 35 non-autistic children (20.3 months) matched on expressive language, yielding 79,229 child turns.
We used Bayesian hierarchical distributional models to estimate group differences and developmental change in five acoustic features, including turn-to-turn variability, and to assess how socialization, language and motor skills relate to acoustic behavior in each group. Using explicit causal graphs to represent our language-matched design, we ran targeted control analyses to assess the impact of age gaps, skill overlap, and session-level speech sampling.
Overall, autistic children showed higher pitch median, greater within-turn pitch variability, faster articulation rate and fewer, shorter pauses than non-autistic children. However, accounting for age removed the pause-count contrast and attenuated the articulation-rate and pause-duration contrasts, while strengthening the pitch differences. When compared across shared skill profiles, the autistic group’s higher pitch variability disappeared, higher pitch and fewer, shorter pauses weakened, and faster articulation persisted. When non-autistic children’s socialization or motor skills increased, they produced lower pitch and smaller pitch swings, respectively, whereas autistic children showed neither association. Across visits, pitch and timing features became increasingly associated in autistic children. Within individual turns, however, there was little covariation in either group.
Group differences in conversational acoustics were present, but their size and pattern varied with age, individual skills, and the acoustic feature examined. These findings caution against treating specific acoustic features as generalizable diagnostic markers and point instead to the need to study how speech acoustics vary with children’s development and interactional contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Motivation to Survival: The Core Psychological Needs Framework as an Allostatic Stress-Regulatory System
articles_hidden.authors: Jozsef Szanto; András Láng
articles_hidden.abstract:
The Core Psychological Needs (CPN) framework is a biopsychosocial model integrating Spitz, Goldfarb and Bowlby’s observations of institutionalized children with evolutionary and neurobiological perspectives. The model proposes that these needs emerge from biological regulatory systems and co-regulate physiological functioning.
Cross Level Construct Decomposition was used to operationalize the theoretical model. Data was collected from 213 participants using chain-referral sampling and ten pre-validated measures prepared using back-translation. Item reduction was conducted using exploratory factor analysis (EFA), followed by structural equation modelling (SEM).
The model showed good fit (CFI = .93, TLI = .91, RMSEA = .053). Safety explained 72.4% of the variance (R² = .724) and showed positive associations with Affiliation (β = .47), Predictability (β = .40), and Control (β = .34), while Social Information showed a significant negative association with Safety (β = −.47). No multicollinearity was identified (VIF < 5).
These findings provide preliminary evidence for the proposed five-factor structure and the central role of Safety. Interpretation within the BOTSA neurobiological framework suggests potential regulatory and compensatory relationships among dimensions; however, these mechanisms remain theoretical given the present empirical evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Reports of Childhood Maltreatment Depend on Current Affect: A 16-Year Population-Based Follow-Up of the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire
articles_hidden.authors: Patrick Jern; Reneé Mustakallio; Annika Gunst; Marianne Källström; Sabina Lehtinen; Pekka Olavi Santtila; Joshua M. Tybur; Martin Lagerström
articles_hidden.abstract: Retrospective reports of childhood maltreatment are widely used in research and clinical settings, yet little is known about the long-term stability of these reports in adulthood. We investigated the consistency of adults’ recollections of childhood maltreatment over 16 years in 1,696 Finnish adults who completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire–Short Form (CTQ-SF) in two population-based surveys in 2006 and 2022. All CTQ-SF subscales showed substantial stability (latent r = .71–.86), but only 4% of participants responded identically to all items. Contrary to expectations, participants did not report less maltreatment overall in 2022; instead, the reports became more dispersed, and more participants reported believing that they had been abused. Depression and anxiety symptoms on each occasion were associated with reporting more maltreatment on that occasion, particularly emotional abuse and neglect, consistent with mood-congruent memory processes. These findings highlight the importance of considering current psychological functioning when interpreting retrospective maltreatment reports.

articles_hidden.title: A 20-minute time-on-task manipulation increases cognitive demand but does not impact x-ray screening performance.
articles_hidden.authors: Callum O'Malley; Amy Gear; Leanne Simpson; Mark Wilson; Samuel James Vine
articles_hidden.abstract: This study examined whether a 20-minute, sustained time-on-task protocol to induce cognitive fatigue affects x-ray baggage screening performance and perceived cognitive demand. Thirty-six untrained participants (15 female) completed two laboratory sessions involving watching a nature documentary (control) or an incongruent, cue-driven Stroop task (experimental). Participants rated cognitive fatigue, motivation, and boredom before and after each manipulation, then completed a 96-image, two-dimensional, x-ray screening task. Performance was assessed using total correct responses and signal-detection metrics (e.g., d'), and response times. Post-task, individuals rated the perceived demands of the task through an adapted task load index. Cognitive fatigue increased from pre-post experimental manipulation and was higher after the experimental than control condition (p=.004). Motivation did not differ between conditions, although boredom was higher post-manipulation in the experimental versus control condition (p<.001). Participants’ x-ray screening performance was similar between conditions (p^' s=.076-.684). Perceived cognitive demand was higher after the experimental condition compared to the control (means 65.5 versus 59.1 a.u.). Our targeted investigation of time-on-task effects on x-ray screening performance indicate novices can maintain their threat detection accuracy when cognitively fatigued by a prolonged time-on-task manipulation. However, time-on-task-related fatigue is linked to increased cognitive resource demands to sustain the same level of x-ray screening performance. To continue the momentum of this emerging field, we advocate for a combination of laboratory assessments, analyses of real-world data, and quasi-experimental studies to inform the aviation security sector of time-on-task and related fatigue effects on x-ray screening performance and how these findings can shape policy and training practices.

articles_hidden.title: Why Adults with ADHD Are Inconsistent Rather  Than Slow: A Computational Phenotyping  Framework Integrating Drift Diffusion Modelling and  Machine Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Abhishek Kumar; Rashmi Gupta
articles_hidden.abstract:
Reaction-time variability (RTV) is a well-established indicator of ADHD, but we still do not fully 
understand its cognitive roots in adults. We analyzed Continuous Performance Task (CPT-II) data from 99 
adults from the HYPERAKTIV dataset (50 ADHD, 49 controls). Analysis combines behavioral analysis, 
drift diffusion modeling (DDM), and interpretable machine learning classification in a single framework. 
Average reaction time did not differ between groups (0.39 s vs. 0.39 s, p = 0.8820), but RTV was 
significantly higher in the ADHD group (0.130 s vs. 0.098 s, p = 0.0026, d = 0.62), which indicates 
attentional instability rather than overall slowing. DDM analysis indicated differences in two components 
of the modeled response process: ADHD participants showed lower drift rates (4.499 vs. 4.782, p = 0.0224, 
rrb = −0.241), which reflects less efficient evidence accumulation, and shorter non-decision time (0.145 s 
vs. 0.172 s, p = 0.0033, rrb = −0.346), suggesting altered non-decision processes. Boundary separation did 
not differ between groups. Drift rate was correlated with childhood symptom severity on the WURS after 
FDR correction (r = −0.302, p = 0.016), and non-decision time was the only DDM parameter that 
independently predicted diagnosis (β = −15.064, p = 0.0073). Classification primarily depends on 
behavioral features (SVM-RBF: ROC-AUC 0.784, 74.2% accuracy), which outperformed DDM-only 
models (best ROC-AUC 0.694, 72.2% accuracy). A Random Forest model combining behavioral and 
DDM features achieved the highest ROC-AUC overall (0.808), but at lower accuracy (71.1%). To evaluate 
feature selection without selection-induced optimism, we performed nested five-fold cross-validation 
across all 511 non-empty subsets of nine behavioral and DDM-derived features. The selected feature 
subset varied across outer folds, with mean reaction time and accuracy selected most frequently. Overall 
nested cross-validation yielded 72.2% accuracy, 72.3% balanced accuracy, and ROC-AUC of 0.772. These 
findings suggest that adult ADHD is characterized more by response inconsistency than generalized 
slowing, with DDM providing complementary information about altered evidence accumulation and non-
decision processes, while behavioral measures remain the strongest basis for classification.

articles_hidden.title: Trust from mistrust: How mistrust can turn gullibility into rational trust
articles_hidden.authors: Mark Alfano; Steven Bland; Michal Klincewicz; Robert M Ross
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we explore the social dynamics of trust, mistrust, trustingness, and trustworthiness in communal settings. In a well-functioning group or institution, especially a group dedicated to inquiry (e.g., scientists, journalists), systematic mistrust by enough people ensures that the outputs of group inquiry are trustworthy, which in turn means that default trustingness – even gullibility – outside of one’s area of expertise is a reasonable disposition or stance to adopt. At the same time, this means that in a poorly-functioning group that lacks systematic mistrust by enough people, default trustingness or gullibility is not rational. We argue that philosophers should reject as too stringent any assumption that default trustingness amounts to irrationality for three reasons. First, whether default trustingness is irrational depends on the norms and practices of the social epistemic structure in which one finds oneself. Second, people are often justified in trusting even when some might regard that trust as irrational. Third, we should be more stringent in policing epistemic norms, and in empowering, honoring, and rewarding what Nietzsche calls the “police of mistrust.” This is because default trustingness is only rationally justified when such mistrust is systematic and those who do the policing are not discredited.

articles_hidden.title: Autism Research's Green Screen: Representationalism and the Political Economy of 'Normal' Environments
articles_hidden.authors: Sahana V Rajan
articles_hidden.abstract:
Responding to Travis LaCroix's diagnosis of the theory-of-mind (ToM) deficit model of autism as a degenerating research program, this commentary examines what remains unasked even when researchers call for better instruments, methods, and autistic-led research. While frameworks such as the double empathy problem and the neurodiversity paradigm expose the ToM model's theoretical fragility and challenge the pathologization of difference, autism research continues to treat neurotypical "normal" environments as a neutral backdrop—a green screen. This commentary interrogates the representationalist assumptions and political economy underlying those environments, arguing that social understanding cannot be evaluated apart from the material and institutional settings in which interaction occurs.

Note: This is an original manuscript of an article published by Taylor & Francis in Psychological Inquiry, Vol. 36, No. 4, pp. 300–305 (published online 27 February 2026), available at: https://doi.org/10.1080/1047840X.2025.2605594

articles_hidden.title: Worlding the Self: The Ecological Constitution of the Pattern Theory of Selflessness
articles_hidden.authors: Sahana V Rajan
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper develops the ecological dimension of the pattern theory of selflessness (PTSL), reconceptualizing its six transformations (T1–T6) as organism-environment enactments. Drawing on ecological psychology and enactivism, it argues that ecological processes are constitutive rather than merely causal contributors to self-pattern transformation: affordances, affective scaffoldings, and social ecologies are not contextual backdrops but co-creators of each transformation. Integrating a relational account of affordances and the distinction between the landscape and the field of relevant affordances with the PTSL's six-transformation model—and drawing on canonical Buddhist sources and ethnographic research on Thai, Burmese, and secular practice contexts—each transformation is shown to involve a distinct mode of ecological participation, from ethical consolidation (T1) and engineered ecologies of attention (T2) to cross-contextual mindful awareness (T3), withdrawal of ordinary self-scaffolding (T4), flexible organism-environment coupling (T5), and irreversible ecological reorientation in self-liberation (T6). Taking the organism-environment system as the unit of analysis specifies testable empirical signatures that distinguish the constitutive hypothesis from causal alternatives.

Note: Preprint (Author's Original Manuscript) of an article accepted for publication in Mindfulness (Springer Nature, 2026). Version of Record: https://doi.org/10.1007/s12671-026-02980-x

articles_hidden.title: Do Children Infer Expertise from Others’ Acts of Imitation?
articles_hidden.authors: Anushka Laha; Zoe A Gipson; Dana Sofia Beas Alvarado; Jennifer Li; Brandon Matthew Woo
articles_hidden.abstract: In everyday life, popular people’s fashion decisions drive fashion trends, leaders inspire collective action, and experts guide decisions broadly. That is, people often imitate those with expertise. In three experiments (N = 249), we investigated whether 4- to 7-year-old children view imitation as a signal of expertise. Specifically, we presented children with interactions in which one agent was imitated and another agent was not imitated, and we investigated whether children selectively learn from the imitated agent. Across experiments, we varied whether the agents were animated shapes, cartoon humans, or real humans. When the agents were animated shapes or cartoon humans, there was either weak evidence or no evidence that children selectively learned from the imitated agent. By contrast, when the agents were real humans, children selectively learned from the imitated agent. These findings support the possibility that, when children observe acts of imitation in person, they make inferences about who has social influence and expertise, and these inferences guide children’s decisions about whom to learn from.

articles_hidden.title: Does music improve or impair cognitive task performance? A Stage 1 Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Maite M. Dechering; Patrick E. Savage
articles_hidden.abstract: Music is an integral part of our everyday lives, often listened to while working or studying. Yet there is a paradox in the literature about whether music improves or impairs cognitive task performance. The arousal-mood hypothesis and the Mozart Effect argue that music improves cognitive task performance, while the duplex mechanism of attention argues that music (particularly music with lyrics) impairs cognitive task performance. Importantly, no adequately powered experiments have compared cognitive task performance for music with and without lyrics against silent and spoken control conditions.  This Registered Report aims to address this through an online experiment investigating cognitive performance on spatial reasoning, arithmetic, and reading comprehension tasks during and after listening to music (including classical, pop, rock, and hip-hop, all with and without English lyrics) or silent or spoken controls (including audiobooks and podcasts). We will test three confirmatory hypotheses (some of which contradict each other): H1: listening to instrumental music during cognitive tasks will improve performance relative to silence; H2: listening to music with lyrics during a cognitive task will impair performance relative to silence; H3: listening to instrumental music during cognitive tasks will be equivalent to performance during a speech condition. Three pilot studies (total n=22) and simulations suggest that the methodology and analysis are feasible, with  an a priori Bayesian design analysis suggesting that 1000 participants are required in the stage 2 study to have an 80% probability of finding compelling evidence (BF10 > 3) for a smallest effect size of interest of d = 0.3. Regardless of whether results support or refute our hypotheses, they will have important implications for recommendations about if/how to listen to music while studying or working.

articles_hidden.title: How large must a shared systematic be to explain the Hubble tension? A hierarchical Bayesian tipping-point meta-analysis of late-Universe H0 measurements
articles_hidden.authors: Nicolás Sánchez-Álvarez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Context. The local (late-Universe) measurements of the Hubble constant disagree with the value inferred from the early Universe under ΛCDM.
Whether the disagreement reflects new physics or an unrecognised systematic error depends on how heterogeneous and how correlated the local
measurements are, questions that are routinely addressed in research synthesis outside astronomy.
Aims. We ask how large a shared, unrecognised systematic would have to be to dissolve the tension, and whether any single method, team or
geometric anchor can carry it.
Methods. We performed a hierarchical Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis of 14 local H0 measurements from 9 methods published in 2020–
2026, with two levels of heterogeneity (between methods and between analyses within a method) and an explicit covariance for shared calibration
components (the NGC 4258, LMC and Milky Way anchors, and common supernova and galaxy samples). Hypotheses were compared with Bayes
factors computed by nested sampling. We then performed tipping-point analyses that solve for the size of a ladder-wide systematic, of a bias in
each geometric anchor, and of the between-method heterogeneity required to reduce the tension to 2σ. As a complement, we refit the expansion
history to the Pantheon+ supernovae, DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations and compressed Planck distance priors.
Results. The pooled local value is H0 = 72.50 ± 1.00 km s−1 Mpc−1, in 3.9σ tension with the early-Universe reference (H0 = 68.41 ± 0.29) and
3.9σ to 5.0σ across four early-Universe references. Between-method heterogeneity is small (τm = 0.74; 90% upper limit 1.9 km s−1 Mpc−1). No
single method drives the result: leaving out each method in turn gives 3.2–4.1σ. Reducing the tension to 2σ requires an unmodelled ladder-wide
systematic of κ∗ = 2.40 km s−1 Mpc−1 (3.3% of H0), about 3.3 times the published anchor-level uncertainty, or a between-method heterogeneity
of τ∗
m = 5.6 km s−1 Mpc−1. A bias in a single anchor would need to be 3.5σ (NGC 4258), 11.3σ (LMC) or 24.0σ (Milky Way) of its published
uncertainty; a bias common to all three anchors would need to be 3.5%. In the expansion-history fit, a magnitude offset of the calibrator supernovae
(∆M = 0.164±0.031 mag) and a 3.7% reduction of the sound horizon are equally favoured over ΛCDM (∆ ln Z = 11.6 and 12.2), whereas evolving
dark energy is disfavoured (∆ ln Z = −3.0) under broad priors.
Conclusions. If the tension has a systematic origin, the systematic must be shared across essentially all distance-ladder routes and be several
