times larger than currently budgeted; method-specific errors of the size suggested by the observed scatter cannot account for it. We also show that
quantum-gravitational corrections to the expansion rate are suppressed by (ℓP H/c)2 ≲ 10−113 at recombination and cannot supply the few-per-cent
change required in the early-Universe route

articles_hidden.title: Tectonic Physiology: Isostatic Containment Mechanisms as a Third Allostatic Regime in Neurodivergent and Other High Processing Cost Phenotypes
articles_hidden.authors: Simone Hauck; Luciana Terra de Oliveira; Pricilla Braga Laskosky
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals with neurodivergent and other high processing cost phenotypes (HPCPh)—marked by pronounced cross-domain functional disparity—frequently experience severe functional collapse, burnout, and migrating somatic symptoms despite routine blood panels deemed “normal.” Whether an adaptive, reversible multisystem regime—Third Allostasis—operates hidden inside ordinary clinical testing remained unmapped. Here we chart 921 chronological panels across 41 anonymized HPCPh individuals (21 longitudinal series; 20 independent multi-laboratory referrals), analyzing inflamed draws separately and measuring within-person mobility against healthy-population normal biological variation benchmarks (European EFLM/EuBIVAS 95% and 99% Reference Change Values). Beneath an intact structural crust (preserved albumin and normal median HbA1c), 37 of 41 individuals engaged core containment axes (water–solutes, iron, adrenal, or thyroid), rising to 19 of 22 engaging three or all four axes where cryoscopic osmometry was measured. Excursions rose and fell symmetrically (212 versus 195 steps), reverted rapidly across clinical thresholds, and took turns across consecutive panels—revealing an isostatic physiology legible only longitudinally within the person.

articles_hidden.title: anvala: A GPU-Accelerated Python Library for Latent Variable and Network Psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Frederico Gonçalves Pedrosa
articles_hidden.abstract:
Applied psychometric modeling has long centered on R packages such as lavaan, semTools, and EGAnet. By contrast, contemporary computational and generative psychometrics, which relies
on large language models and dense text embeddings executed through tensor operations, runs predominantly in Python. Passing data and model specifications back and forth between the two
environments adds serialization overhead and makes reproducible pipelines harder to maintain. At the same time, resampling-intensive methods such as bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa)
bootstrapping and bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis (boot_ega) remain slow when executed sequentially on standard processors. Here, I introduce anvala (v0.1.0), an open-source Python
library built on PyTorch that matches the numerical output of established R psychometric packages while using graphics processing unit (GPU) tensor parallelization to accelerate resampling. Adopting lavaan-compatible model syntax and double-precision (float64) automatic differentiation, anvala supports continuous (ML, MLR) and ordinal (WLSMV) structural equation modeling, multigroup measurement invariance testing with partial invariance and Lagrange multiplier score tests, bifactor reliability indices, and network psychometrics (EGA, Unique Variable Analysis, and entropy fit indices). On canonical benchmark datasets, anvala reproduces R reference parameter estimates, robust standard errors, scaled fit indices, and network structures within 10−16 to 10−5 across factor, ordinal, multi-group, bifactor, and network models, and within 1.10 × 10−4 on the small-sample full SEM. Three simulation studies then map the CPU–GPU performance crossover across model dimensionalities (p ∈ [3, 60]) and confirm 100% convergence, low parameter bias (< 5%), wellcalibrated interval coverage, and accurate latent mean recovery under partial invariance.

articles_hidden.title: Workplace Inclusion Measures for Neurodivergent Teachers: A Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Jessica Spiegler; Norah Richards; Anna Melissa Romualdez; Liz Pellicano
articles_hidden.abstract: Inclusive school practices, especially for students who are neurodivergent and have special educational needs, have received important attention in recent years. Yet, little is known about the inclusion of those tasked with upholding these practices for students, the teachers themselves. Disabled teachers perceive their firsthand experiences as fostering inclusive schools. There is a growing body of literature reporting on workplace experiences of neurodivergent teachers, such as those who are autistic, ADHD, and dyslexic, yet the systems and cultures that support their workplace inclusion have not been addressed. This study aimed to review what is known about the supports and structures that foster or prevent workplace inclusion for neurodivergent educators. In total, thirty-nine studies about teachers and pre-service teachers who are autistic, ADHD, and have specific learning disabilities such as dyslexia were included in this review. We analysed these deductively, drawing upon critical social theory, and inductively, to present a thematic synthesis of the systems and cultures that contribute to the employment inclusion and exclusion of neurodivergent teachers. Teachers often used their firsthand experiences of neurodivergence to renegotiate attitudes and assumptions within school cultures to foster inclusion for both their students and themselves. They experienced exclusion when navigating systems that were not bolstered by broader inclusive cultures and where systems were prioritised over culture. Rapport with colleagues and students were described as key for maintaining inclusion. We identify a need to focus on the relational and cultural dynamics that determine how inclusion is negotiated within school workplaces.

articles_hidden.title: Music on the mind: Changes in prefrontal cortical activity and prosocial behavior related to a pilot communal music-based intervention
articles_hidden.authors: Pooja Mathur; Eneyse Pinheiro; Deborah Wanderley dos Santos; Vanessa Pancheri; William Teixeira; Mariana Stochero; Suelen Galdino; Luisiana Baldini Franca; Patricia Vanzella; D.Phil. Jill Miranda Hooley
articles_hidden.abstract: Positive well-being outcomes are associated with prosocial behavior. Understanding how cortical activity relates to changes in prosocial behavior can guide the development of interventions for those with neural deficits in prosocial behavior and support measurement when self-report may not be possible. This pilot study explored how a communal music-based intervention may relate to improvements in prosocial behavior and its relationship with cortical activity to establish feasibility and generate hypotheses for larger trials using hypothesis-driven and exploratory analyses. 37 children aged 4-6 were randomly assigned to a control group (visual art-focused, passively listened to music) or treatment group (communal music engagement) for 10 sessions of 45 minutes each. Hemodynamic responses were assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy collected pre- and post-intervention while participants listened to communal vs. unknown music. Prosocial behavior was measured with parental reports via the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. We found initial differences in cortical activation, particularly in the superior frontal gyrus, between the control and treatment groups using bootstrap resampling methods (b = -11.470, 95% CI = [-21.202, -2.126]). We also found that the same area was correlated with changes in prosocial behavior (ρ(28) = 0.490, p = .008). Correcting for multiple comparisons eliminated some significant findings. These pilot study findings suggest a need for further exploration with refined hypotheses to better understand relationships between communal music engagement, improvements in prosocial behavior, and cortical activity. There is an opportunity to expand on this research with a larger sample and a longitudinal design.

articles_hidden.title: Video games in cognitive event-related EEG research: A scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Belinda Fleischmann; Sean Mulready; Dirk Ostwald
articles_hidden.abstract: Event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on controlled laboratory tasks with limited ecological validity. Video games offer a middle ground between laboratory and real-world settings, combining intuitive interaction with experimental control. Despite growing interest, the use of video games in event-related EEG research has not been systematically charted. This scoping review characterizes the video game paradigms used and relates the reported findings to canonical laboratory effects. Database and supplementary searches identified 29 studies using 26 paradigms. Most paradigms used custom-built games and required visuomotor navigation or targeting within continuous gameplay, and most analyses were time-locked to feedback events such as hits or collisions. Findings showed selective convergence with laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, and for movement-related activity. Evidence for error- and feedback-related components was more limited, while early sensory responses were rarely examined. We discuss emerging patterns in the use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms, the correspondence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, and the methodological challenges of studying event-related activity during gameplay. In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about neural responses during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.

articles_hidden.title: Generational Differences in Postpartum Mental Health in the 21st Century: A Cohort Comparison of Dutch Parents
articles_hidden.authors: Caro Henrica Catharina Lemmen; Fangxiang Mao; Frank C. P. van der Horst; Rianne Kok; Maartje Luijk
articles_hidden.abstract: The prevalence of maternal mental health problems seems to have increased since the start of the 21st century. Several societal changes may have contributed to this increase, most notably increasing individualism, rising perfectionism and intensification of parenting norms. The current study examines how postpartum mental health and associated factors changed over time by comparing two birth cohorts collected fifteen years apart in the same city. The study found comparable feelings of anxiety and depression during the first six months postpartum among mothers in 2002-2006 and 2017-2021. For both cohorts, lower levels of social support and more perceived infant sleeping problems were associated with poorer postpartum mental health, whereas infant sleep characteristics (e.g. sleep duration) were not. The strength of these associations did not differ between cohorts. Although infant sleep characteristics were similar across cohorts, a higher proportion of mothers in the 2017-2021 cohort perceived their infant’s sleep as problematic. This may reflect increasing expectations of parenthood in a changing sociocultural context. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding maternal mental health not as the result of individual vulnerabilities but in relation to the context of how parents experience everyday parenting challenges and the support available to them.

articles_hidden.title: Social Influence on Reducing Animal-Based Food Consumption: A Mixed-Methods Scoping Review
articles_hidden.authors: Nina van den Broek; Rosaly Severijns; Maud Rolleman; Junilla Larsen; Esther K. Papies
articles_hidden.abstract:
Social influence is widely recognized as an important determinant of food consumption, yet evidence on reducing animal-based food consumption is dispersed across disciplines, study designs, and social influence concepts. This mixed-methods scoping review provides a comprehensive overview of 124 studies assessing social influence on reducing or lower animal-based food consumption in upper-middle and high-income countries since 2000.
We systematically searched seven databases for studies examining social influences on animal-based food consumption and the adoption or maintenance of reduced animal-based diets. Quantitative and qualitative evidence was synthesized separately and subsequently integrated.
 This growing body of literature remains concentrated in specific countries and demographic groups. The quantitative synthesis (N = 73) revealed 10 studied social factors, of which social norms are most often studied, with stronger evidence emerging from observational than experimental research. Qualitative studies (N = 51) revealed the social processes and contexts through which dietary change occurs, including negotiation of conflicting preferences, practical and emotional support, social pressure, and the influence of shared meals and social contexts. The integrative synthesis suggests that social influence is best understood as a multifaceted and context-dependent phenomenon operating across interpersonal and broader environmental levels.
Future work should seek to better understand how multiple forms of social influence interact across contexts and populations, and should prioritize creating conceptual clarity when describing these phenomena. Doing so will likely require greater use of mixed-methods, social networks, and context-sensitive approaches capable of capturing the complex social realities through which dietary change occurs in daily life.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Mere Jealousy: The Experience of Relational Boundary Violations in Three European Cultures
articles_hidden.authors: Hadi Shaban-Azad; Roger Giner-Sorolla; Afroditi Pina; María del Carmen Herrera Enríquez; Iraklis Grigoropoulos; Antonio Herrera; María Dolores Sánchez Hernández
articles_hidden.abstract: In Western cultures, jealousy is felt when a valued relationship is feared to be lost to a rival. The Middle Eastern near-cognate emotion gheirat calls our attention to a broader range of relational boundary violations (RBVs) which are worthy of study as social emotion appraisals. This qualitative study takes a step back from specific emotion words to examine reactions to RBVs in European dignity and honour cultures, including the innovation of situations that would elicit gheirat but not jealousy. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in the UK (N = 24), Spain (N = 21), and Greece (N = 24), and analysed using hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis. Results revealed a shared tripartite structure across all three samples. Relational rivalry and harm elicited identical experiences of jealousy and protectiveness. However, relational intrusion showed cultural differences, producing an unlabelled and elusive experience among British participants, discomfort among Spanish/Greek women, and territoriality among Spanish/Greek men. Meta-belief themes (emotion regulation, reputational concerns, gendered norms, and generalised mistrust) showed greater cultural variability than phenomenological themes, aligned with gheirat's honour-related, moralised, and gendered characteristics. Together, these experiential and interpretive patterns inform our understanding of gender-based relational violence in European contexts, beyond the narrow label “jealousy”.

articles_hidden.title: Jargon as a Psychological Construct? A Multidecade Analysis of Communication Failure in Evaluation Reports
articles_hidden.authors: John Hite
articles_hidden.abstract: For seven decades, studies have asked whether the people who receive psychological evaluation reports understand what they say. Existing research has largely measured reader satisfaction rather than what readers comprehend, recall, or interpret. This narrative synthesis identified six studies, conducted between 1984 and 2025 in school psychology and, most recently, child neuropsychology, in which 253 readers were assigned to a standard-format report and had their comprehension scored directly. Comprehension ranged from 46.6% to 61.1% (weighted mean = 55.2%) and showed no detectable change across four decades. In every study that also scored an accessible version of the same report, readers understood it better, with scores from 60% to 82%. Recent evidence from pediatric neuropsychology shows the same gap: parents rated their understanding of their child's report highly, yet almost half could not state the child's diagnoses without error. Effective formats combined plain-language wording with one or more of domain-based organization, concrete behavioral examples, and elaborated recommendations. These findings suggest that jargon-related comprehension failure is a persistent, measurable, and modifiable problem spanning specialties within psychology. Implications for training, supervision, and evidence-based communication practice across school and clinical psychology are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and acceptability of Ever-Steady, an AI-supported conversational coaching app for exercise engagement in Parkinson's disease: a single-arm mixed-methods study
articles_hidden.authors: Wesley Pyke; Aliya Saleem; Osman Onur Cil; Luma Tabbaa; Izzy Wellings; Gurprit Lall; David Wilkinson; Jim Ang
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Regular exercise confers benefits for motor symptoms and quality of life in Parkinson's disease; however, long-term adherence remains a substantial challenge. Ever-Steady is a web-based application, co-produced with people with Parkinson's, that combines personalised goal setting, conversational activity logging with an artificial intelligence (AI) coaching companion ("Mr Steady"), weekly progress summaries, and curated educational and follow-along exercise content.
Objective. To evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of Ever-Steady and to explore preliminary changes in exercise motivation and Parkinson's-specific quality of life.
Methods. A single-arm, pre-post, mixed-methods feasibility study was conducted. Adults with Parkinson's disease were recruited through a community-based therapy centre in Kent, United Kingdom, and were asked to use the application for eight weeks. The Behavioural Regulation in Exercise Questionnaire (BREQ-3) and the 39-item Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39) were administered at baseline and follow-up. Acceptability was assessed using a post-intervention evaluation questionnaire and semi-structured interviews, which were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis.
Results. Nine participants were enrolled; one withdrew before using the application, and all eight who commenced the intervention completed follow-up (100% retention; mean age 69.9 years). Seven participants reported using the application on at least four days per week, seven agreed that it integrated readily into daily life, six would recommend it to another person with Parkinson's, and five reported an increase in exercise, with none reporting a decrease. Intrinsic motivation for exercise increased by 0.41 points on a 0 to 4 scale (95% CI 0.09 to 0.72; dz = 1.08), whereas controlled forms of motivation were unchanged. The PDQ-39 Summary Index improved by 1.5 points in the full sample (non-significant) and by 5.2 points (p = .004) in a sensitivity analysis excluding one participant whose follow-up responses were inconsistent with their concurrent evaluation and interview data. Five themes were generated: making activity visible; from intention to action; a companion that listens; recognising effort; and fitting around life with Parkinson's.
Conclusions. Ever-Steady was feasible to deliver and acceptable to the majority of participants, and its use was associated with a large, exploratory increase in intrinsic motivation for exercise. Participants identified specific refinements, namely effort-sensitive feedback, persistent goal visibility, reliable voice interaction, wearable integration and peer connection, which will inform the next development cycle and support progression to a larger controlled evaluation.

articles_hidden.title: The Psychology of Algorithmic Bias
articles_hidden.authors: David Michael Amodio; Tessa Elizabeth Sadie Charlesworth; William J. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: Algorithmic bias—the systematic discrimination of disadvantaged social groups by AI systems—is widely documented, yet its psychological foundations remain poorly understood. We argue that algorithmic bias originates primarily from human prejudice and social cognition, which shape AI training data and use of AI systems. We introduce the psychology-centered Human–AI Loop model that explains how biases can enter an AI system during its creation and consumption, specifying the psychological mechanisms operating at each entry point. These mechanisms and their interactions create feedback loops through which AI systems amplify, perpetuate, and obscure existing prejudices and social inequalities. We then outline psychology-informed strategies for disrupting these cycles and discuss implications for theories of prejudice and discrimination in the age of AI.

articles_hidden.title: Starting Young: The Gender Gap in Policy Attitudes Is Already Evident in Adolescence
articles_hidden.authors: Nikki Dekker; Bert N. Bakker; Anke Munniksma; Remmert Daas; Han L. J. van der Maas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Political polarization along gender lines is well documented among adults, but it remains unclear how early the gender gap is evident and whether it extends beyond broad ideological identification to specific policy issues. We examine gender differences in policy attitudes among Dutch adolescents aged 12–18 in a sample broadly representative of the population in terms of gender and age (N = 1,697; 52% girls; 42% lower secondary school). We assess gender differences across 15 policy issues, within-gender polarization, and ideological profiles identified through latent class analysis. 

We find a systematic gender gap, with boys consistently expressing more conservative views than girls. Importantly, the magnitude of this gap varies across policy
issues and is strongly associated with whether an issue is gender-related (rpb = .66). Gender differences also extend beyond mean attitudes: boys show greater within-group polarization on gender-related issues than girls. Latent class analyses further identify distinct ideological profiles, with girls more likely to be classified as progressive (54% vs.16%) and boys as conservative (37% vs. 10%). Together, these findings show that gender differences in policy attitudes are already evident in adolescence, highlighting adolescence as an important stage for research on interventions addressing gender-based political polarization.

articles_hidden.title: Walking over a bridge makes humans undershoot the way home
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Roy; Katharina Wünning; Timo Oess; Marc Ernst
articles_hidden.abstract: As surface-travelling animals, humans are thought to encode vertical space coarsely, a view rarely tested during real locomotion. Here, blindfolded participants walked an outbound path, either flat or over a bridge, then returned to the start along a straight, flat path. In Experiment 1, they returned accurately after the flat path but stopped short of home after crossing a bridge, opposite to the overshoot expected from measuring distance along the walked surface. Contrary to coarse coding, homing after the bridge was no less precise than after the flat path. Experiment 2 tied the undershoot to vertical movement itself: it occurred over bridges with different inclinations and over stairs with horizontal treads, and more than tripled when participants crawled over the bridge, whereas a matched flat path left homing unaffected during walking. The undershoot may stem from the well-known overestimation of slopes: participants indeed overestimated every bridge’s inclination, and their perceived slopes explained most of the mean error in Experiment 1, but not all results. Vertical movement thus appears to be processed metrically, like horizontal movement, but from biased perception. This bias, often thought to leave action unaffected, may therefore shape how we find our way home.

articles_hidden.title: Teacher’s perceptions of positive traits and strengths in children with neurodevelopmental conditions
articles_hidden.authors: Amy De Roubaix; Jennifer de Smidt; Lessa Madelief Schippers; Martine Hoogman
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Research on neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs) has traditionally emphasized challenges rather than strengths. Existing strengths research primarily covers on ADHD, autism, and Specific Learning Disorder (SLD), with limited attention to Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) and Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). Moreover, strengths are typically studied within single diagnostic groups, despite the frequent co-occurrence of NDCs, and most studies rely on adult self-reports or parent reports. Little is known about teachers' perspectives on strengths in children with NDCs, despite their unique opportunity to observe multiple children at once and in both academic and social contexts. Method. In this mixed-methods study, we explored teachers' perspectives on positive traits in children with NDCs. Sixteen teachers completed semi-structured interviews and the Signature Strengths Survey, indicating whether 24 character strengths were characteristic of  specific NDCs. Qualitative data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis.
Results. Teachers identified 22 positive traits across children with NDCs, clustering into five domains: cognitive skills, self-regulation and efficacy, social and interpersonal skills, practical skills, and energy-related traits. Most traits were reported across diagnostic groups, some were reported uniquely in children with ADHD or autism. We described a conceptual framework on the development and use of positive traits comprising compensatory, promotive, protective, and double-edged mechanisms.
Conclusions. The findings highlight the diversity of positive traits identified by teachers and their context-, recipient-, and intensity dependent nature. By extending the limited literature across NDCs, this study contributes to a more balanced understanding of neurodevelopmental differences and may inform strengths-based educational and clinical approaches.

articles_hidden.title: Parenting Beyond the Gender Binary: A Scoping Review to Better Conceptualize Gender-Neutral Parenting
articles_hidden.authors: Joyce Endendijk; Miriam Holzer; Emma Spruit
articles_hidden.abstract: Objective: Recently, there has been an increasing societal and scientific interest in gender-neutral parenting as a means of challenging societal gender norms and achieving equal treatment of people regardless of their gender. Yet, the scientific literature on gender-neutral parenting is fragmented, using different terms and definitions. The present scoping review aimed to clarify how gender-neutral parenting is defined and conceptualized across childhood and adolescence. Design: Following PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews, a systematic search of the literature published until September 2025 was conducted across different search engines (e.g., Web of Science, Scopus, PsycInfo). In total, 34 publications met predefined eligibility criteria. The content of the publications was analyzed using a hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis in NVivo. Results: Across publications, we identified 9 parenting dimensions that clustered within four interrelated systems of action: (a) counter-stereotypical role modelling and reinforcement; (b) disrupting, expanding, and de-centering gender schemas; (c) supporting children’s gender agency and self-determination; and (d) reshaping gendered systems beyond the family context. Together, they form a coherent constellation of parenting practices that we conceptualize as gender-expansive parenting, a term that provides a better fit to the different dimensions than the term gender-neutral parenting. Conclusion: By offering a clear conceptualization and theoretical integration of gender-expansive parenting, this review lays the groundwork for the development of assessment tools and empirical research on how gender-expansive parenting practices shape children’s gender development and well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Adverse Childhood Experiences and Trauma-Informed Meditation: A Narrative Review
articles_hidden.authors: Aisha Ijlal; Sebastian Ehmann; Marco M. Zierhut; Kerem Böge; Matthew D. Sacchet
articles_hidden.abstract: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are now considered significant predictors of rehabilitation as they shape regulatory capacity, trauma vulnerability, and engagement in treatment across the life course. This narrative review synthesizes recent research on ACEs, trauma-informed care, contemplative practice, and rehabilitation to explore how developmental adversity can affect the delivery, tolerability, and rehabilitative worth of meditation-based interventions. The review draws on peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2026 from PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, and Web of Science, while retaining limited earlier sources for conceptual grounding. The literature indicates that mindfulness- and meditation-based interventions support trauma recovery by improving emotional regulation, self-compassion, and related recovery processes. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous. Trauma burden and contextual instability may influence benefit and adverse effects. Across correctional, substance use, women-focused, and community re-entry settings, contemplative practice appears most useful when adapted through trauma-informed principles, including safety, pacing, and ongoing monitoring of tolerability. The review therefore argues that meditation in rehabilitation cannot be delivered as a generic intervention but must be matched to trauma burden and functional recovery goals. Drawing on a framework of meditative development, the progressive deepening of self-regulatory and attentional capacities through contemplative practice, the review further proposes that trauma is not only a risk factor for contemplative practice but may serve as a site of resolution and growth when practice is appropriately staged, supervised, and supported. An ACEs-sensitive model of meditative development offers a more clinically useful framework than generic contemplative delivery for diverse implementation settings.

articles_hidden.title: The Coherence Problem: Integrating Computational, Phenomenological, and Network Accounts of Psychopathological Transformation
articles_hidden.authors: Joël Kuiper
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychotic and affective states alter not only what a person thinks and perceives, but how coherently their experience hangs together. Phenomenological, computational, network-neuroscience, and dynamical-systems traditions have each characterized aspects of this alteration, but largely in isolation from one another. This paper argues that these traditions converge on a shared control problem. If inference on the brain's recurrent architecture tends toward self-reinforcing certainty, as the paper proposes, then the system must continuously counteract that drift or experience reorganizes. Bipolar disorder provides the clinical lens because it resists the compartmentalization the field has imposed: the condition can produce manic, psychotic, depressive, and mixed configurations, and no account designed for one configuration readily extends to the others. A minimal decomposition, targeting the entry, propagation, and temporal depth of coherence, maps these psychopathological presentations as neighboring regions in a shared space and reframes the explanatory question: which control policies sustain proportionate coherence in ordinary cognition, and how they destabilize.

articles_hidden.title: Whose Experiences Are Represented in Autism Research? Looking at Who Takes Part in Australian Autism Research and How They Are Described
articles_hidden.authors: Dawn Adams; Megan Walsh; Timea Molnar; Kate Simpson; Simon Bury; Halle Wiblen; Chris Paradisis
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite a growing body of autism research, significant gaps remain regarding whose experiences are reported, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of representation across the evidence base. This systematic mapping review examined demographic reporting and representation of autistic participants in Australian autism research published between 2023 and 2025. Searches across 46 academic databases identified 517 Australian autism empirical research articles, of which 467 involved human participants and 272 included demographic data for autistic participants. Demographic reporting of included articles was examined using the PROGRESS-Plus framework alongside priority and intersectional groups identified in Australia's National Autism Strategy. Gender/sex and age were the most frequently reported characteristics, appearing in 89.3% and 74.6% of articles, respectively. In contrast, reporting for First Nations identity, cultural background, socioeconomic status, intellectual disability, communication profiles, sexual orientation+ status, and very high support needs were considerably less common. Eligibility criteria also shaped representation, with many studies requiring a formal autism diagnosis and some excluding participants based on English proficiency, English literacy, intellectual disability, communication profile, or non-speaking status. These findings indicate that many autistic participants remain demographically invisible in autism research, limiting the understanding of whose experiences underpin the evidence base. More consistent demographic reporting, clearer justification of exclusion criteria, and more accessible recruitment and participation methods are needed to support equity, transparency, and policy relevance in autism research. While this study focused on the Australian context, the findings may reflect broader challenges in demographic representation and reporting within autism research internationally.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Properties of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale-12 (IUS-12) Among University Students in Ho Chi Minh City
articles_hidden.authors: Nguyen Trung Phan; Le Anh Thuan; Nguyen Tran Le Uyen
articles_hidden.abstract: Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is a transdiagnostic risk factor associated with various mental health problems, and the 12-item Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS-12) is the most widely used instrument to measure this construct. However, a review of published studies identified no psychometric evaluation of the IUS-12 in Vietnam. This study aimed to examine the factor structure, reliability, and gender measurement invariance of the IUS-12 among university students in Ho Chi Minh City. A total of 536 undergraduate students participated in the study, of whom a subsample of 120 completed a retest after two weeks. Factor analysis indicated that the two-factor model demonstrated an acceptable fit and clearly outperformed the unidimensional model. Configural and metric invariance across gender were supported, and partial scalar invariance held after freeing the intercepts of two items. The total scale and both subscales demonstrated good internal consistency and satisfactory temporal stability over a two-week interval. Overall, these findings provide initial evidence on the internal structure and reliability of the IUS-12 among students in Ho Chi Minh City, although its relations with other constructs remain to be tested.

articles_hidden.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles_hidden.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles_hidden.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles_hidden.title: A Practical Guide to Adapting Evidence-Based Treatments into Digital Single-Session Interventions for Youth
articles_hidden.authors: Atina Manvelian; Monika Neff Lind; Ian Sotomayor; Arielle C. Smith; Joanne Davila; Jill Ehrenreich-May; Juan Pablo Zapata; Jessica L. Schleider
articles_hidden.abstract: Most young people with mental health disorders do not receive any mental health care. Digital single-session interventions adapted from evidence-based treatments help address this problem by making potent therapeutic skills widely accessible. There is increasing demand and interest in developing digital single-session interventions, yet there is no guide to promote best practices. Objective: This paper guides readers through the development of effective, self-guided, digital single-session interventions for youth. Method: We convened eight researchers with extensive experience developing, testing, and disseminating digital single-session interventions for youth. This team collected and distilled lessons learned from over a dozen single-session intervention projects into this guide. Results: This paper has four parts: an introduction to demonstrate the value of single-session interventions, a step-by-step guide for developing effective single-session interventions, a case study demonstrating how we followed the steps in the development of a single-session intervention, and answers to frequently asked questions. The step-by-step guide breaks down the development process into five phases. During the preparation phase, we cultivate a single-session mindset. During collaboration, we assemble the right team to reach our target audience. During adaptation, we select an evidence-based treatment and a proven, standalone component to feature. During design, we create the content of the single-session intervention. Finally, during engagement, we use best practices to increase uptake and learning. These phases are summarized in a supplemental single-session intervention development checklist. Conclusion: This manuscript serves as a guide for the creation of effective, scalable, self-guided, digital single-session interventions for youth.

articles_hidden.title: Continuous Tracking of Subjective Visibility
articles_hidden.authors: María; Daniel Sanabria; Francisco Garre-Frutos
articles_hidden.abstract: A salient target can vanish from awareness for seconds, right before our eyes, when a pattern moves around it. Does the target switch off like a light, or does it fade away? This phenomenon, known as motion-induced blindness (MIB), is often described as an all-or-none experience, but this characterization rests largely on measures that capture only whether the target is visible or invisible, rather than how its visibility changes over time. In a preregistered experiment, we measured target visibility using classic button presses, a concurrent continuous measure (a slider moved while viewing the display), and a retrospective measure, Temporal Experience Tracing (TET), in which participants reconstructed their experience after each trial. All three methods were reliable, sensitive to a manipulation of target visibility (its eccentricity), and highly correlated across participants. Beyond mean visibility, the continuous methods captured how visibility changed over time. Using the slider, participants tracked an objective change in visibility with a lag of only 0.2 s. Computational modeling of subjective visibility dynamics revealed that visibility neither switched off like a light nor simply faded away, but instead shifted gradually between two alternating states. Traces reconstructed from memory were less precise and less extreme than online reports, yet most parameters describing these dynamics were correlated across methods. Continuous reports thus capture what button presses cannot, and what people report online and reconstruct from memory share not only how visible the target was, but also aspects of how its visibility changed over time.

articles_hidden.title: White matter microstructure in schizophrenia-spectrum and clinical-high-risk samples: an umbrella review of diffusion tensor imaging evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Ayla Ihsan; Ather
articles_hidden.abstract: While reduced fractional anisotropy (FA) on diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is the most consistently reported finding in psychosis, whether these alterations precede the first episode and progress with illness stage, and whether the review evidence can answer this, is unresolved. We carried out an umbrella review that covered systematic reviews and meta-analyses, appraising the quality of every included review with the AMSTAR-2 tool. We also built an evidence map that charts what the published reviews conclude about white matter microstructure by tract and illness stage, measured how far the reviews share primary studies, and tested how stable their agreement is. In total, 17 systematic reviews and meta-analyses of standard-tensor DTI were included, and all were of critically low quality. Their 460 citations covered only 235 unique studies, so apparent agreement among reviews reflects shared data, not independent replication. Although 24 of 27 cells covered by three or more reviews were majority-reported as reduced FA, only 12 held across all thresholds, and 54 of 75 votes came from narrative reviews, including every clinical-high-risk cell. Taken together, the reviews report reduced FA in the corpus callosum, cingulum bundle and long association tracts in clinical-high-risk, first-episode and mixed schizophrenia-spectrum samples. Stage-specific alterations in early psychosis and in chronic schizophrenia could not be confirmed. Whether white matter alterations progress across illness stages could neither be supported nor refuted. Whether medication, sex or age moderate these alterations is largely unexamined in the reviews to date.

articles_hidden.title: Writing near to the patient’s experience: narrative techniques for collaborative clinical note-writing
articles_hidden.authors: Sarah Kathryn Fineberg; Nicole Campbell; Kate Jones; Jiwoo Han; Ryan Amer; Alexandra Alario; Rosa Shapiro-Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a commentary written to describe the use of literary techniques to support collaborative clinical note writing in mental healthcare.

articles_hidden.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Acoustic Startle Response in Autism Spectrum Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Renee Leow-Guerville; Ala Seif; Jeffrey Chen; Mohammed Rajab; Kimya Moeini; Aaliyah St. Denis; Susanne Schmid; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract:
Sensory processing differences are nearly universal in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with
auditory hyperreactivity being among the most commonly reported by Autistic individuals. The
neural mechanisms underpinning these auditory differences are unclear, and previous research has
been mixed. We performed a systematic review and multilevel meta-analysis across measures of
the Acoustic Startle Response (ASR) thought to differ in ASD: acoustic startle reactivity, pre-pulse
inhibition (PPI), and habituation. Despite mixed findings in the literature, our meta-analysis
revealed increased reactivity, decreased PPI, and no significant difference in habituation in ASD
compared to their neurotypical peers. However, it is difficult to draw generalizable conclusions
about habituation due to heterogeneity in habituation measurement. Future work to standardize
ASR testing is needed to gain a comprehensive understanding of the neurophysiological processes
driving these effects.

articles_hidden.title: Redistributive Values may be Shaped by the Interaction Between Country-Level Factors and Individual Traits
articles_hidden.authors: Panagiota Tsilogianni; Elijah Paul Galvan; Alan Sanfey
articles_hidden.abstract: Although economic inequality is often perceived to pose a substantial threat, public support for redistributive policies is often mixed – with substantial variation in support for redistributive policies seen across countries. These findings point to the importance of understanding how preferences for redistribution are shaped by a combination of system-level influences and individual traits. To address this important question, we employ a multimethodological design: studying redistribution both via behavioral decision-making in a laboratory task and also via opinions on real redistributive policies. In a large, online sample (N = 240) of participants in a cross-national study, we find converging evidence from both behavioral and political data that both cultural values (i.e. individualism-collectivism) and economic experiences (i.e. relative redistribution) jointly predict preferences for redistribution, though these effects were relatively weak. Probing further into trait-and-system interactions, we find that moral concerns for proportionality (i.e. moral foundations questionnaire 2) strongly moderated these effects. In particular, the data suggest that, in individualistic contexts, greater relative redistribution may, surprisingly, lead individuals who care more about meritocratic fairness to prefer greater redistribution. A productive aim of future research on the psychological motives underlying redistributive behavior may, therefore, be to further explore how system-level factors interact with individual-level traits.

articles_hidden.title: Automating Personality Research with LLMs
articles_hidden.authors: Elisa Altgassen; Annika Iris Külpmann; Ruben C. Arslan; Björn Erik Hommel; Rui Mata; Dirk U. Wulff
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to reproduce central aspects of human personality. This correspondence creates opportunities to automate research, but its theoretical value will depend on what LLMs recover and what accounts for their discrepancies with human data. We propose a heuristic distinction between model-derived variance--the regularities in human personality data recoverable from LLM predictions—and residual variance--the structure that remains unexplained by those predictions. LLM-human correspondence may reflect several factors, such as general semantic structure, culturally shared beliefs, scientific findings in LLM training corpora, or psychometric fine-tuning. Residual variance, in turn, may reflect model limitations, population-specific variation, or psychological information not captured in language. Using this distinction, we examine three applications in personality psychology with substantial potential for automation: enhancing assessment, improving conceptual clarity, and simulating human respondents. Current evidence suggests that linguistic representations account for a substantial share of LLM–human correspondence, with psychometric fine-tuning providing additional gains; however, the relative contribution of other factors remains unresolved. We argue that automation can contribute to conceptual progress to the extent that the sources and limits of LLM–human correspondence are identified. Doing so can establish what similarities and divergences reveal about personality itself and where automation is justified.

articles_hidden.title: The Heart the Lord Sees: Representing Moral Motivation in Biblical Commands, Teachings, Parables, and Narratives With the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA) Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Scripture rarely evaluates action apart from the heart that produces it. The
Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA) framework represents a moral motivational
state as four independent, continuous dimensions formed by crossing motivational
direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad): Approach
Good, Avoid Good, Approach Bad, and Avoid Bad. This article applies MoMA to
biblical commands, the teachings of Jesus, parables, and the narratives of prophets,
kings, warriors, and disciples. I argue that biblical moral discourse consistently
highlights the distinctions MoMA was built to preserve: reluctance versus temptation,
conflict versus indifference, identical acts done from different hearts, and repentance
as a change in what is perceived as good. The analysis yields integrative contributions
including a representation of Gethsemane as conflict without sin, a distinction
between sanctification and metanoia, a reading of divine pedagogy as dimension-
specific intervention, and testable predictions for counseling, formation, and the
psychology of religion.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the N400: Testing behavioural and neurophysiological predictors of political voting intention
articles_hidden.authors: Zoja Michelle Repovš; Georgios P.D. Argyropoulos; Jan Kuipers
articles_hidden.abstract: Identifying unbiased measures of political attitudes is crucial for comprehending the electorate and their needs. Recent studies have examined the capacity of the N400 Event-Related Potential to implicitly measure (dis)agreement with political statements, with mixed results. We sought to assess the predictive capacity of the N400 beyond the binary electoral options investigated thus far (e.g., pro vs. against Brexit) to the UK’s multi-party electorate. Participants rated their agreement with politically charged statements while their EEG brain responses to those statements were recorded. Consistent with earlier observations, statements that participants disagreed with elicited a more negative N400 than statements they agreed with. However, manual agreement ratings did not align with party preference and N400 amplitude was unreliable as a predictor for voting intention in a multi-party context. Alternatively, MVPA of EEG data showed that the level of agreement with a political statement could be predicted above chance, albeit within and beyond the N400 time-window. This suggests that, MVPA of all scalp electrodes may be more successful than the N400 in predicting voting intention within the context of multi-party electoral contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Speech production and vocal interactivity are linked to infants' development of a consonant bias in wordform processing
articles_hidden.authors: Irene Lorenzini; H. Henny Yeung; Anthony Picaud; Thierry Nazzi
articles_hidden.abstract:
Speakers in many languages show a processing bias for consonants in word learning and recognition
(C-bias). Infants learning such languages initially display an opposite bias for vowels (V-bias),
switching to the C-bias through experience with native phono-lexical properties. In French-learning
infants, this switch happens between 6 and 8 months. Here we asked whether early phonetic
production is linked to this developmental pattern. Thirty-one French-learning 7-month-olds
completed a wordform segmentation task testing consonant-vowel perceptual biases, daylong
recordings (LENA system), and parental questionnaires. This procedure captured several production
measures, including: a) the variety of consonants produced (human-coded); b) consistency in
consonant production (Vocal Motor Schemes); c) interactivity of vocal productions in social settings
(LENA’s machine-coded estimate ‘Conversational Turns Count’, and the Vocal Reactivity Scale of
the Infant Behavior Questionnaire); as well as d) the frequency of canonical babbling vocalizations
(LENA’s estimate ‘Child Vocalization Count’). Results confirmed no group-level bias at this age,
consistent with an ongoing developmental transition. Subsequent statistical analyses of individual
variability revealed complex effects of phonetic production on the emergence of the C-bias, with a
significant 2-way interaction between variety of consonants produced and interactivity of vocal
productions. Surprisingly, this interaction revealed that more advanced production skills were
negatively linked with the emergence of the C-bias in infants who do not benefit from frequent vocal
interactions in their social environments. This result highlights complex relationships between early
phonetic production and phono-lexical processing, showing that perception/production links can be
modulated by social interaction.

articles_hidden.title: Frontotemporal and parietal theta and beta synchronization support musical pleasure and motor learning
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander William Albury; Marc Deosdad Díez; Gemma Fàbrega-Camps; Alberto Ara; Josep Marco; Virginia Penhune
articles_hidden.abstract: Music perception and performance involve a broad range of cognitive processes related to prediction, pleasure, and action planning. Each of these processes and behaviours recruit distinct brain areas, and these brain areas must communicate with each other to coordinate complex behaviours such as learning to play an instrument. One theorized mechanism supporting this interregional coordination is synchronization of neural oscillations. Theta- and beta-band activity in particular have been identified as being related to music reward and motor planning, respectively. In this study, we measured oscillatory activity using EEG while non-musicians performed a passive listening task and piano learning task. Using Bayesian regression models, we measured the relationship between intersite theta synchronization and liking ratings, and intersite beta synchronization and motor learning accuracy and asynchrony. Replicating previous research, we found that theta synchronization between right frontotemporal areas was positively associated with participant liking ratings. We also observed long-range theta synchronization between right frontal and parietal areas. In beta, we found that synchronization in right frontotemporal areas was associated with motor learning accuracy, and synchronization in parietomotor areas was associated performance asynchrony. These results provide evidence for the role of theta-band activity in music reward and suggest that processes of evaluation are supported by communication between a broad network of regions in the dorsal and ventral auditory streams. The results also highlight the role of beta-band activity in supporting pitch-to-key mapping and timing accuracy during motor learning in music.

articles_hidden.title: Person-Specific Models for Short-Term Prediction of Suicidal Ideation in Adults With Depression From Ecological Momentary Assessment and Passive Sensing
articles_hidden.authors: Ahhyun Lee; Anna M Langener; Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Michael V. Heinz; Tess Z Griffin; Matthew David Nemesure; Damien Lekkas; Arvind Pillai; Amanda C Collins; Subigya Nepal
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Suicidal ideation changes within hours and varies across individuals. However, the accuracy of the short-term personalized (i.e. idiographic) prediction remains modest and how we can improve the model has not been systematically appraised.
Aims. We examined whether near-term suicidal ideation can be predicted within individuals, and whether multimodality, dynamic features and model structure improve prediction.
Method. We built personalized short-term prediction models on suicidal ideation in 143 adults with major depressive disorder. Models used 90 days of ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and passive sensing data from smartphones and wearables. Each model forecast the 4-hour item 9 rating at a prompt from data ending 4 hours earlier, and evaluation was retrospective. Models varied in data type, feature construction (mean-based or dynamic) and window length; continuous and two-part hurdle models were compared.
Results. Idiographic models showed weak discrimination (median AUC .51 to .55, best model .55, 95% CI .50 to .57). They beat the below-chance training-mean baseline on AUC but not on R², and the previous-day mean matched the best model’s AUC (.554 vs .552). Multimodality and dynamic indices each improved AUC by at most .02. Person-specific windows did not improve discrimination over fixed windows. Hurdle models had lower absolute error, mainly on prompts without ideation.
Conclusions. Personalized short-term prediction models showed weak accuracy, consistent with prior literature. Richer features including multimodality and dynamic features did not improve prediction beyond simple benchmarks. The lower error of hurdle models mostly reflected predictions close to zero.

articles_hidden.title: The Quantitative Psychologist Is Dead, Long Live the Quantitative Psychologist
articles_hidden.authors: Sacha Epskamp
articles_hidden.abstract:
Much of what quantitative psychologists publish consists of developing statistical methods, implementing them in software, and evaluating them in simulation studies. I argue that artificial intelligence (AI) can already do much of this work, and that its share will only grow. The quantitative psychologist has always been a jack of all trades, combining programming, statistics, and psychological knowledge without being a master of any one of them. AI is now the better jack of all trades. When methods become cheap, value moves to what AI cannot supply and to what it newly makes possible. I describe three directions: collecting trustworthy data from real people, formalizing psychological theory now that computational modeling is within reach of any researcher, and rethinking methodological education
so that students learn to judge the analyses that AI will run for them. The
specialist role built around producing methods for others will fade, while
quantitative thinking spreads through all of psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Give-a-number task scoring methods influence the observed number knowledge
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The Give-a-number (GaN) task is used to determine the symbolic number knowledge of children when they initially acquire the meaning of the number words. Precise measurement of number knowledge is essential because even small measured differences in the development process may lead to fundamental theoretical consequences. The task has several variations, and these versions are usually considered equivalent. However, recent works have raised the issue that different versions may classify children differently, which has been partially confirmed. Here, to extend these initial studies, the role of the various scoring methods of the task, that is, how the number knowledge is calculated given the task responses, was investigated. It was found that the scoring method considerably influences the observed number knowledge, and the effects of the various scoring method components are added up. These results demonstrate that the specific scoring method influences the validity and reliability of the measurement. These differences affect the comparability of studies using different methods of the GaN task, and various versions lead to differing observed patterns that, in turn, may lead to differing theoretical conclusions.

articles_hidden.title: Certain Minds in an Uncertain World? Exploring Computational Signatures of Belief Updating in Individuals Holding Radical Attitudes
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Knorr; Nikita Podolin; Alexander Starlinger; Małgorzata Kossowska; Nace Mikus
articles_hidden.abstract: Radical political attitudes have been linked to rigid beliefs, a pattern commonly understood as reflecting motivational processes that promote the defense of valued beliefs and identities. Emerging evidence suggests that this rigidity also manifests in how individuals process politically neutral information, suggesting a domain-general rigid cognitive style. The computational basis of this cognitive style, however, remains largely unknown. We investigated the computational correlates of radical attitudes during learning under uncertainty using a politically neutral predictive-inference task in 462 US adults. Dogmatic intolerance and authoritarianism, two radical-attitude dimensions derived from a battery of political-attitude questionnaires, were both associated with overconfidence. We also found weak evidence that dogmatic intolerance was associated with poorer predictive performance, but no evidence that either radical-attitude factor was associated with impaired metacognitive sensitivity. Computational modelling indicated that dogmatic intolerance, but not authoritarianism, was selectively associated with a more changeable representation of environmental volatility. This raises the possibility that dogmatic-intolerant belief systems are sustained by allowing contradictory experiences to be explained away as changes in the environment rather than as challenges to existing beliefs. Together, these findings suggest that heightened subjective certainty may coexist with more labile representations of environmental regularities, pointing to a computational signature of dogmatic intolerance.

articles_hidden.title: Recruitment and retention in randomised controlled trials involving autistic adults: a systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Jade Eloise Norris; Nicola Mills; Dheeraj Rai; Alba X Realpe
articles_hidden.abstract: A significant body of research highlights physical and mental health inequities faced by autistic adults. However, randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with autistic people are often underpowered, with this population considered ‘difficult to recruit’. This systematic review aimed to examine recruitment and retention to RCTs with autistic adults, as well as synthesising strategies used to facilitate recruitment and retention. MEDLINE, PsycINFO, EMBASE, CINAHL, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases were systematically searched for RCTs recruiting autistic adults published to June 2023, with a second search conducted in December 2025. ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry were also searched. We report details for N=47 trials, including type of intervention and control, planned and achieved recruitment and retention rates, and strategies to maximise these. Included studies focused on improving e.g., social skills, cognition, mental health, quality of life, employment, and driving skills. Findings are reported in a narrative synthesis, showing a proliferation of trials recruiting small samples, wide ranging recruitment and retention rates, and a paucity of information regarding target sample sizes and/or power calculations. Facilitators of recruitment and retention included integrating Patient and Public Involvement and co-production, involving family/carers, public advertising and accepting self-referrals, remote participation, and reasonable adjustments.

articles_hidden.title: Semantic structure and measurement in large language models for psychopathology and psychometrics
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Raballo; Michele Poletti; Antonio Preti
articles_hidden.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reconstruct item-item associations and subscale structure in psychopathology questionnaires from the semantic and sentiment embeddings of item text. Responding to Kambeitz et al. (Nature Mental Health, 2025), this finding extends beyond representation: the linguistic composition of psychometric instruments may help shape the covariance observed in responses, not only reflect latent constructs. Convergent work in semantic psychometrics indicates that item semantics can be used operationally, supporting item-level questionnaire completion from unstructured text, cross-scale prediction, and diagnostic inference. Implications for questionnaire redundancy, instrument harmonization, and language-based adaptive assessment follow. Semantic structure cannot, however, replace empirical validation, clinical judgment, or longitudinal and interventional evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Linguistic Variation in Wrap-Up Effects Reflects Adaptive Sensitivity to Information Structure
articles_hidden.authors: Inbal Kimchi; Amit Avigdor; Leon Hager; Paul van den Broek; Sascha Schroeder; Victor Kuperman; Noam Siegelman
articles_hidden.abstract: The wrap-up effect, i.e., the inflation of reading times on sentence- or clause-final words relative to preceding words, is a robust finding in reading research, typically interpreted to reflect integrative processing of meaning. However, recent cross-linguistic evidence has cast doubt on its generalizability across languages, raising questions about the mechanisms that underlie it. Here, we test an information-theoretic account of the wrap-up effect, according to which the effect reflects readers’ adaptive behavior to where semantic information resides in their written language. We start by showing in a large-scale text reading database (N=1,234 from 20 languages) that there is, in fact, systematic cross-linguistic variation in wrap-up effects. Then, we use sentence-embeddings to quantify languages’ trajectories of semantic informativeness in sentence endings, showing that they closely align with the observed cross-linguistic variability in wrap-up effects. Specifically, languages with increasing informativeness in sentence endings also show canonical wrap-up effects, whereas languages with declining informativeness patterns have no or reversed effects. Lastly, we show that these correlations are driven by readers’ general expectations regarding the structure of their written language. This is revealed by models showing that global (i.e., language-specific mean) informativeness trajectories rather than local (i.e., sentence-level) changes predict the magnitude of the wrap-up effect in a given sentence. Together, these findings provide a novel interpretation of the mechanisms underlying the wrap-up effect, positioning it as a consequence of learning computations that readers use to assimilate their writing system’s structure, thus offering a principled explanation for its cross-linguistic variability.

articles_hidden.title: Predictive Significance Testing: A Complement to Coefficient Significance in Confirmatory Linear Regression
articles_hidden.authors: Gyeongcheol Cho
articles_hidden.abstract: Across disciplines, linear regression is used to examine hypothesized effects of treatments, interventions and other exposures. Conventional significance tests ask whether population regression coefficients are zero, but do not directly assess the size or practical importance of these effects. A different question is whether estimated effects improve predictions for new observations. An effect can be nonzero yet fail to improve prediction when uncertainty in its estimated coefficient outweighs the predictor's unique signal. Here we introduce predictive significance testing to answer this question within a prespecified linear regression model. We measure the change in expected prediction error when a predictor's fitted contribution is removed at prediction time, without refitting the model. This differs from earlier comparisons of separately estimated forecasting models. Under specified assumptions, we derive an unbiased estimator and a predictive p value that is exactly calibrated at the boundary of no net predictive benefit. We also derive nonzero, sample-size-dependent thresholds for familiar regression effect-size measures that distinguish positive from negative predictive contributions. Simulations support the procedure's statistical performance, and an empirical illustration identifies a predictor that is coefficient-significant but not predictively significant. Together, these results distinguish evidence for a nonzero regression effect from evidence that its estimate improves prediction.

articles_hidden.title: Automating Reproducibility Checks Using Large Language Models
articles_hidden.authors: Yoel Inbar; David Tannenbaum
articles_hidden.abstract: Computational reproducibility checks are essential to scientific credibility, yet few published papers are ever independently verified, largely because manual checking is labor-intensive and time-consuming. We tested whether an agentic large language model (LLM) could perform computational reproducibility checks at scale. We benchmarked computational reproducibility checks performed by an LLM analyst (Claude Opus running in the Claude Code harness) against results from expert-led reproducibility audits in the social and behavioral sciences and found that LLM accuracy was comparable to that of human experts. Agentic LLMs can now perform high-quality reproducibility checks relatively cheaply, quickly, and easily, putting large-scale audits within reach for journals, granting agencies, organizations, and individual researchers.

articles_hidden.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles_hidden.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles_hidden.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a large number of surveys being distributed was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles_hidden.title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee; Gregory Russell Samanez-Larkin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: Coordinated Psychological Intervention Ensembles Outperform Single-Mechanism Designs Across Societal Challenges
articles_hidden.authors: Anandita Sabherwal; Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu; Elke U. Weber
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral science tends to seek the single most predictive explanation for behavioral phenomena and subsequently the most effective intervention for behavior change. Yet many consequential outcomes, from climate action to democratic attitudes, result from multiple psychological processes, raising the question of whether combining interventions that leverage different processes would prove more effective. Across a 13-intervention megastudy and a second, megastudy-informed experiment (Ns = 8,488 and 2,547 US adults; both quota-matched and preregistered) we test whether intervention ensembles—deliberate combinations of distinct psychological modules delivered together—can more effectively shape target behaviors and attitudes.  We test three principles for constructing such ensembles: 1) outcome optimizing ensembles (combining top-performing individual interventions), 2) mechanism coverage ensembles (covering key psychological drivers of the outcome), and 3) multi-level synergy ensembles (combining individual-, collective-, and system-level processes). Ensembles consistently outperformed their constituent single-mechanism interventions. In Study 1, relative to an informed control, the strongest ensemble increased climate policy support by 41.5% and donation by 43.0%. And in Study 2, the ensemble was significantly more effective than its components in reducing partisan animosity and strengthening democratic attitudes. The largest gains were achieved by multi-level synergistic ensembles that aligned processes across individual, collective, and systemic levels. LLM-assisted analyses of participant reasoning reveal that effective ensembles work by resolving complementary psychological barriers, not by simply providing more arguments. For complex societal challenges shaped by multiple barriers, interventions can achieve behavior change at greater rate and scale by designing coordinated intervention ensembles rather than by searching for the single best mechanism.

articles_hidden.title: Legislative Inconsistencies in Defining Psychology Registration in the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld): Mandatory Reporting and Implications for Provisional Psychologists
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Paul Sullivan
articles_hidden.abstract: 2021 amendments to the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld) in Queensland to criminalise the non-disclosure to police of child sexual abuse (CSA) (s229BC) had consequential implications for the practice of psychology, particularly psychotherapy. Where patients make self-disclosures about current or historical CSA perpetrated against them by an adult when they were a minor (including historical CSA in a now adult patient), psychologists, like all adults in Queensland are required to report that to police, unless one of the “reasonable excuses” against disclosure applies. This paper discusses the wording in the Act with a focus on relevant reasonable excuses in the therapy context, and how the Act contains ambiguity in the application of the law to psychology trainees who are provisional, rather than student registrants under the national health practitioner regulatory scheme.

articles_hidden.title: A decision support toolkit for AI-ready neuroscience data governance
articles_hidden.authors: Wilhelmina M. Botes; Artur Mendes; Bart Huffman; Madison Fleischaker; Ciara Staunton; Beverley Townsend; Paul Ogendi; Lukman Abdulrauf; Andrea Parziale; Gabriela Skoczylas-Kizak
articles_hidden.abstract:
Contemporary human neuroscience relies on exchanging and analyzing neurodata across global institutions and
jurisdictions. However, regulatory architecture fails to maintain continuity of protection across distributed research
environments. Our comparison of 93 countries and 10 operative governance units across Africa, Europe, Latin
America and the Caribbean, and North America shows that neurodata are rarely recognized as distinct regulatory
objects, usually falling under broader legal classifications. While international sharing is permitted in principle,
transformation into derivatives, embeddings, and AI models raises questions about the scope and implementation of
continuing safeguards. We show that international exchange is defined by conditional interoperability, where effective
safeguards require aligning legal, institutional, and technical controls. To operationalize these findings, we introduce a
modular governance toolkit for the data-to-model lifecycle, including a Neurodata Risk Classification Framework,
decision support tools for neurodata transfer and transformation, and a Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement to
sustain protection without global legal harmonization.

articles_hidden.title: Error correction necessitates immediate, answer-containing feedback: Challenging error suppression, episodic reinstatement, and semantic mediation accounts
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Folger; Matthew Rhodes; Jexy An Nepangue; Hannah Hausman
articles_hidden.abstract: Generating errors during learning benefits subsequent recall, particularly when corrective feedback is presented immediately. Feedback in existing research conflates notification of error commission with provision of the correct target. Across two experiments, we examined the effects of immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and delayed feedback with an immediate “error” warning on cued and error-cued recall. In Experiment 1, warnings did not mitigate the detrimental effect of delayed feedback on cued recall, indicating that optimal pretesting requires immediate, answer-containing feedback. This challenges two hypotheses of errorful learning: that suppressing errors at encoding facilitates error correction (the error-suppression hypothesis), and that error commission promotes context binding which enables episodic reinstatement during feedback and at test (episodic reinstatement hypothesis). Immediate feedback improved cued recall performance but not participants’ ability to recall the accuracy of their initial responses, further contradicting the possibility of episodic reinstatement at test facilitating target recovery. In Experiment 2, delaying feedback improved error-cued recall, undermining mediator-based accounts which assume that errors function as additional retrieval cues, increasing the likelihood of successfully retrieving the target. We propose that error commission increases attention to the target at encoding, strengthening the cue–target retrieval route.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
