memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Is short-term storage correlated with fluid intelligence? Strategy use explains the apparent relationship between ‘number of remembered items’ and fluid intelligence
articles_hidden.authors: Zeljana Babic; Mark Schurgin; Timothy F. Brady
articles_hidden.abstract: Working memory is a core cognitive system that actively maintains information in an accessible state to support a variety of everyday tasks. Working memory performance has frequently been shown to strongly correlate with fluid intelligence, particularly when tasks involve a high degree of manipulation and executive function, as opposed to solely utilizing short-term storage capacity. However, recent work has claimed that simple storage capacity is also correlated with fluid intelligence, and that this is driven by a particularly special and dissociable component of capacity, the ‘number of items represented’ (rather than the precision of those representations). Here we demonstrate that such correlations do not arise solely or primarily from simple storage capacity (nor a single dissociable component of capacity), but are driven by the availability and usage of different kinds of visual representations to represent the stimuli. We found that despite being probed on the same items, with the same foils, at the same set size, only working memory displays that allowed for the use of both item and ensemble representations correlated with fluid intelligence. These results provide evidence against the hypothesis that simple storage alone is related to fluid intelligence. They also demonstrate that participants make use of more complex and structured representations rather than solely individual item representation, even in simple storage tasks, and suggest that strategic utilization of these representations may be, in such situations, what drives correlations with fluid intelligence.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement Trajectories in a Jail-Based Dialectical Behavior Therapy Group
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Stall; Edelyn Verona
articles_hidden.abstract: Jail-based mental health interventions are delivered under conditions of short and unpredictable stays, making treatment engagement difficult to evaluate. Although Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) has demonstrated promise in correctional settings, little is known about how engagement changes over time in jail-based DBT. Participants (N = 325; 84.9% male) were enrolled in a six-week, jail-adapted DBT skills group as part of a larger randomized controlled trial. Facilitators provided weekly ratings of attendance, in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion. Latent Profile Growth Modeling identified engagement trajectories among participants who attended at least three sessions (N = 232), and mixed-effects models examined whether profile membership predicted changes in mental health symptoms and coping. Participants attended an average of approximately 6 of 12 sessions, and 40.2% completed the full cycle. Noncompletion occurred through multiple routes, including release or transfer and the program’s three-miss attendance criterion. Three trajectories were identified: Declining Engagement (37.5%), High-Stable Engagement (29.7%), and High Early Engagement with Drop-Off (32.8%). The High-Stable group had the highest attendance and completion rate. The Declining group showed lower in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion beginning early in treatment, whereas the High Early Engagement with Drop-Off group remained relatively engaged across these indicators before a later decline in attendance. Noncompletion in the latter group was primarily associated with release or transfer. Profile membership was not associated with differential changes in symptoms or coping, although mental health symptoms and maladaptive coping decreased overall. These findings show that repeated engagement measures can distinguish early, broad declines in participation from later interruptions in attendance that would be obscured by completion status alone.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Consensus-Based Ratings to Assess Dimensions of Early Life Adversity: Links to Emotion Regulation and Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Mark S. Chen; Alexis Brieant; Isabella Kate Kate Peckinpaugh; Leila Adames; Ante Dany; Dylan G. Gee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of early life adversity (ELA) posit distinct developmental consequences of threat, deprivation, uncontrollability, and unpredictability. Existing approaches force each event into a single dimension or rely on self-ratings that may conflate exposure with subjective appraisal.
Objective: We evaluated consensus-based dimensional ratings as an alternative and examined their associations with emotion regulation and psychopathology.
Participants and Setting: A Prolific sample (N=200; Mage=23.06; 49.5% female; 48% racial minorities) was used to derive the consensus values; a community sample (N=291; Mage=22.40; 59.5% female; 60.5% racial minorities) was used to test their transportability out of sample.
Methods: In Sample 1, we derived consensus values from averaged ratings of 82 ELA items and compared consensus-based and self-rating scoring (feasibility test). In Sample 2, we applied Sample 1 consensus values (transportability test). Dimension scores—threat, deprivation, unpredictability, uncontrollability—predicted cognitive reappraisal, emotion dysregulation, and psychopathology symptoms.
Results: Uncontrollability and unpredictability were highly collinear with threat and deprivation (VIFs > 50) and thus not retained in regression models. Consensus-based scoring was feasible in Sample 1, and consensus-based associations transported to Sample 2. Deprivation was associated with depression, PTSD, and emotion dysregulation in both samples (R² = .04-.22, ps < .01), and negatively with cognitive reappraisal (p = .007).
Conclusions: ELA dimensions are separable at an event level but entangled at the person level, preventing clean specificity in naturalistic samples noted in the literature. Consensus-based values may offer a way to select samples with distinct exposure profiles, treat self–consensus discrepancies as meaningful appraisal differences, and evaluate whether such appraisals could be intervention targets.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between psychological monitor competency and mental health literacy: A reassessment of Guo et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Guo et al. recently reported statistically significant links in a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) model and interpreted these findings as evidence that psychological monitor competency reinforces mental health literacy among university psychological monitors. However, methodological research has shown that cross-lagged estimates may emerge as artifacts of model specification rather than reflecting genuine prospective influence. To examine the robustness of the reported findings, we reanalyzed the data used by Guo et al. using several alternative analytic approaches. Across specifications, estimated associations varied considerably in both magnitude and direction, with positive, negative, and nonsignificant effects all observed. Meta-analytic aggregation of estimates across models generally yielded effects that were not statistically different from zero. These results indicate that the conclusions advanced by Guo et al. may not be robust and that the apparent prospective associations could be attributable to methodological artifacts. Strong developmental interpretations are therefore not warranted on the basis of the available evidence. We recommend that observational findings, including cross-lagged effects, be evaluated across multiple defensible modeling approaches before substantive conclusions are drawn.

articles_hidden.title: Speaking through shared hubs, not gendered spokes? Exploring sex-related variation in object naming in Tunisian Arabic-speaking people with post-stroke aphasia
articles_hidden.authors: Amina KLIBI
articles_hidden.abstract: Whether sex-related factors shape confrontational object naming in non-Western clinical populations remains understudied within the Controlled Semantic Cognition framework. We evaluated naming performance across eight semantic categories and three overall measures in 14 native Tunisian Arabic speakers with post-stroke aphasia (6 males, 8 females). Group differences were examined using nonparametric Mann–Whitney U tests and Bayesian analyses. Uncorrected comparisons initially favored female patients in Furniture naming (p = .023) and Total Immediate Responses (p = .043). However, no category-level differences survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses predominantly supported the null hypothesis (BF₀₁ = 1.24–2.15), with Furniture showing only weak, inconclusive evidence for a sex effect (BF₁₀ = 1.93). Overall, results provide no convincing evidence of systematic sex-related disparities in object naming. These findings align with a shared amodal semantic hub rather than gendered spokes, though larger studies are required to confirm sex invariance in this population.

articles_hidden.title: The Approximate Number System is an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The approximate number system (ANS) is an imprecise representation of numbers that is widely assumed to support both symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical tasks. It is believed to be not only the foundation for simple numerical operations but also for higher-level mathematical thinking. One fundamental support for the ANS is the existence of the ratio effect in symbolic number comparison. That is, for example, when Arabic numbers are compared, human performance is proportional to the ratio of the to-be-compared values, similar to psychophysical comparison of perceptual features. A critical issue with this account, however, is that an exact operation, which is required in symbolic number comparison, cannot be backed solely by an imprecise representation. This is for several reasons. First, while a psychophysical model assumes imprecise representation, humans can compare symbolic numbers with arbitrarily high precision. Second, psychophysical models predict worse performance for number pairs with a relatively small ratio than the actual human performance. Third, if an additional mechanism supporting exact comparison is also assumed, current empirical evidence cannot verify the ANS model. Fourth, the ANS account differentiates approximate and exact tasks, where only approximate tasks can be solved purely with the ANS. However, the comparison task is assumed to be processed purely by the ANS, even if the task is exact. Taken together, these arguments make the ANS an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison. While these arguments question the role of the ANS in symbolic number processing, the ANS may have a role in nonsymbolic number processing, although the general relevance of the ANS may be considerably lower than assumed by previous works. Consequently, the individual differences in the sensitivity of the ANS may be less critical in higher-level math performance, dyscalculia diagnosis, or training programs.

articles_hidden.title: The Family Criticism Paradigm: A Laboratory Task for Investigating Psychophysiological Responses in Parent–Child Triads
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Investigating stress regulation processes within the family context offers important evidence to understand the development of mental and physical health problems. However, laboratory paradigms for investigating stress in several family members simultaneously are limited. The present study introduces and evaluates a standardized paradigm to investigate psychophysiological responses to family-framed standardized evaluative feedback in parents and children simultaneously. A total of 120 families (consisting of a mother, father, and their child aged 10-12 years) participated in a laboratory session in which they were individually but simultaneously exposed to neutral, praising, and critical audio comments presented as originating from the other two family members. Psychophysiological response was assessed using mood, state rumination, and autonomic nervous system activity measures, including vagally mediated heart rate variability (HRV), pre-ejection period (PEP), and skin conductance level (SCL). Results showed that criticism increased negative affect (tension, sadness, anger) and decreased positive affect in both parents and children. Self-critical rumination increased 5 and 10 min after the exposure to the paradigm. At the physiological level, HRV was lower during both praise and criticism than during neutral comments, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity during social evaluation. During recovery, HRV increased, suggesting a rebound in parasympathetic activity, while sympathetic responses showed decreased cardiac sympathetic activity (PEP) in parents and increased sympathetic activation (SCL) in children. These findings support the use of this paradigm for eliciting affective, cognitive, and physiological stress responses among family members, offering a promising approach for research on stress regulation and resilience within family systems.
